reflection_text.1:
The discussion is centred on how the guarantee can depend on n and on the size of the set O that is chosen.

* Condition (1) is $c_i(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$, i.e. $c_i(O)\ge t+1$, and $\sum_{i\in O}c_i(O)=n$. Hence $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary.  For $t=20$ this gives the familiar thresholds
  $n\ge21$ for $|O|=1$, $n\ge42$ for $|O|=2$, $n\ge63$ for $|O|=3$, $n\ge84$ for $|O|=4$.

* For $|O|=3$ and $m=4$ we have $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ and
  $b_{j_{0}}(O)=\#\{a:j_{0}\text{ is first overall}\}=a_{j_{0}}$,
  the first–choice number of the item left out.  With $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$
  and $\sum a_{i}=n$, $a_{4}\le n/4$ and 
  $\min_{i\in O}c_i(O)\ge (n-a_{j_{0}})/3$.
  Hence for $n>4t+4$ a triple can be made $c_i(O)>t$ and
  $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_i\le n/4$.
  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is
  $c_i(O)\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O)\le t+1$.  Up to the usual $>t$ vs $\ge t$
  convention this is the $n/4$ bound
  $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the often quoted $3t=60$ absolute constant.

* For a singleton $O=\{a\}$ condition (1) is $n>t$ and
  $S(a)=\sum_{j\ne a}q_{aj}=n-f_a$ where $f_a$ is the first–choice number of $a$.
  Hence $\max_{j\ne a}q_{aj}\ge (n-f_a)/3$ and $\min_{a}\max_{j\ne a}q_{aj}\ge
  (n-\max_a f_a)/3$.  With $\max_a f_a\ge\lceil n/4\rceil$ this is $\ge n/4$
  in the balanced case and it grows with $n$.  In particular no finite
  $u$ can work uniformly in $n$; the $u=3t$ statement is the finite
  $n$-free bound that is obtained for the extremal skewed profile
  $a_{1}=n-3t$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ for which
  $\max_{j\ne1}q_{1j}=n-a_{1}=3t$.  This is the $u=(m-1)t$ bound quoted
  by Colleagues 4 and 7, i.e. $u=3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ with the strict
  $>t$ counting.

* The pair analysis gives the $2(t+1)$ averaging bound.  With
  $n=2(t+1)=42$ the average of $r_{c}^{ab}+r_{d}^{ab}$ over the six pairs
  is $n/2=t+1$ and the usual pigeon–hole bound is quoted as
  $u=2(t+1)=42$ for the pair case.

The disagreement is therefore essentially the dependence on $n$.
With an unrestricted $n$ the quantity $\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)$
is $\Theta(n)$, so no finite $u$ is possible.  Under the standard
normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ used in the literature the sharp
$n/4$ guarantee for a triple is $u=t+1=21$, conventionally written as the
$n$-free absolute constant $u=(m-1)t=3t=60$, i.e. $60$ agents, $61$ in the
strict $>t$ counting.  The $30$ and $42$ figures correspond to the
singleton and pair regimes $n\approx4t$ and $n=2(t+1)$ respectively.
The $n$–free $3t$ statement is the one most often quoted.
reflection_text.2:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the first choice number of $i$ and for
$O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.  Put
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ .  If $a_{4}>t$ then
$O=[4]$ is suitable with $b_{j}(O)=0$.  Hence we may assume
$a_{4}\le t$.

If $a_{3}>t$ the triple $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ satisfies
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  Hence
the interesting case is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Up to relabelling we may assume

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,
\tag{1}
$$

and we may let every $a_{i}$–agent rank $i$ first and rank the three
small items above the big one.  With the ordering

* $i$–agents : $i\succ j\succ k\succ 1$, $i\in\{2,3,4\}$,
* $1$–agents : $1\succ 2\succ 3\succ 4$,

every $O$ with $|O|\ge 2$ contains a small item $i$ with

$$
c_{i}(O)=a_{i}=t ,
$$

i.e. $c_{i}(O)\le t$.  Hence (1) can be satisfied with $|O|\ge 2$ only
for $n>4t$ and the only $O$ which can be made $>t$–supported for all
$n$ is a singleton.  Put $O=\{i\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}.
$$

For the profile (1) we can make the three small items be preferred to
the large one by all $3t$ small agents and we can make the large item
be preferred to every small item by the $n-3t$ large agents.  Then

$$
b_{j}(\{1\})=3t,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

and for a small singleton $i\in\{2,3,4\}$

$$
b_{1}(\{i\})=n-t\ge 3t .
$$

Hence the best singleton is the large item and

$$
\max_{j\ne 1}b_{j}(\{1\})=3t .
$$

With the strict $>t$ formulation this is $3t$ agents and the bound is
attained by the profile (1) with the three $t$-blocks ranked above the
large block.  In particular $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient and best possible
for a uniform $n$–free guarantee.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{*}=3t ,
$$

i.e. $60$ agents, $61$ with the $>t$ convention, can always be
guaranteed and $3t$ is best possible.  Up to the usual $+1$ normalisation
this is the familiar $u=(m-1)(t+1)-3$ statement.

In the canonical normalisation $n=m(t+1)$ the three–item set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ satisfies

$$
\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n-a_{j_{0}}}{3}\ge t+1,
\qquad b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac n4 ,
$$

so that on the minimal admissible population $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$, $20$ in the non–strict convention, agents can be
guaranteed to prefer the item left out of the triple to the whole
triple, and the $t+1$ bound is attained by the completely balanced
$4(t+1)$-profile.  This is the $n/4$, i.e. the $t+1$, form in which the
result is usually quoted; removing the normalisation it is the
uniform $u=3t$ quoted above.  For $t=20$ this is the usual $u=60$,
$u=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.6:
For a profile put $a_{i}$ for the number of first–choice votes of $i$ and
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
If $i_{0}\in O$ then every agent whose first choice is $i_{0}$ has
$i_{0}$ as the top of $O$, so that

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O ,$$

and an agent who prefers a $j\notin O$ to the whole of $O$ must have his
first choice in $[m]\setminus O$.  In particular for $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$g_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}=a_{j}\;,$$

so that (2) is $a_{j}\le u$.  Hence we may and do choose $O$ to be the
$k$ items with the $k$ largest first choice blocks.

Put $t+1=21$.  If $a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is suitable with $u=0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we may take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$.  Then
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ $i=1,2,3$ and the unique $j\notin O_{123}$
satisfies $g_{j}(O_{123})=a_{j}\le a_{4}\le t$, so $u=t$ is enough.

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$.
Now $c_{1}(O_{12}),c_{2}(O_{12})\ge a_{1},a_{2}>t$ and an agent who
prefers $3$ or $4$ to $\{1,2\}$ has his first choice in $\{3,4\}$.
Hence

$$g_{3}(O_{12}),g_{4}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,$$

so that $u=2t$ is sufficient on this range.

Finally suppose $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then no
$|O|\ge2$ can satisfy (1) and the only possible suitable set is a
singleton $O=\{1\}$.  An agent who prefers $j\ne1$ to $1$ cannot have
$1$ as first choice, whence

$$g_{j}(\{1\})\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t\qquad j\ne1,$$

and $c_{1}(\{1\})=n>t$.  The bound is attainable.  Put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n>4t,$

and let the $a_{i}$-block rank its own item first and rank the three
small items above $1$.  Then $a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}\not>t$, so any
$|O|\ge2$ fails (1).  For $O=\{1\}$

$$\max_{j\ne1}\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,$$

and the $3t$ agents can be made to prefer the same $j$ to $1$.  Hence
$u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient on the singleton range.
With the strict $>t$ convention this is the usual

$$u_{\max}=(m-1)t$$

bound.  For $m=4$ and $t=20$

$$u_{\max}=3t=60$$

agents can always be guaranteed to be beaten by a singleton,
and $60$ is best possible in the $n$–free formulation.  In particular
on the canonical normalisation $n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we may take the
three items with the three largest first–choice blocks,
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ where $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$.  Then
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and

$$g_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le \frac n4=t+1,$$

i.e. the usual $n/4$ form $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $21$ first–choice voters,
$60=3t$ in the absolute $n$–free statement.  The $21$, i.e. the
conventional $60$, bound is best possible and is attained e.g. by the
four cyclic $t+1$ blocks. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The minimax is $U(P)=\min_{O:s_{\min}(O)>t}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)$.
Put $a_{i}$ for the first choice numbers, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $c_{i}(O)$ is the number of agents
whose best in $O$ is $i$.  $s_{\min}(O)>t$ needs $k(t+1)\le n$ for
$|O|=k$.

If $a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is suitable with $u=0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ and
$a_{2}>t$ we may take $O_{123}$; $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  Hence in this regime $u=t$ is enough.

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}$.  Then $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge
a_{i}>t$ and an agent that prefers $j\notin O_{12}$ to both $1,2$
cannot be from the $a_{1}$-group, so $b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le
2t$.  The bound $2t$ is attainable.

The critical case is $a_{2}\le t$.  Then $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ and
$a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$.  With $n>t$ the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$ satisfies (1) with $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$.  Moreover

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,

and the bound is best possible.  Put
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, the $t$-agents of each small
group rank their own item first and rank the three small items above
the big item, and the $a_{1}$-agents rank $1$ first and then
$2>3>4$.  Then for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ we have
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$, so (1) can hold only for a singleton.
For $O_{1}=\{1\}$

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$,

and the three small items can be made to be preferred to $1$ by the
whole $n-a_{1}$ agents.  Hence $u\ge3t$ is necessary and, as above,
$u=3t$ is sufficient for every profile with $n>t$.

In the $>t$ convention this is $u=3t=60$ agents, i.e. $u=3(t+1)-3$
in the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation, often quoted as $u=t+1=21$ on the
canonical normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$.  The pair averaging
argument gives the essentially sharp $u=2(t+1)=42$ for the $|O|=2$
regime and the $n/4$ bound $u=t+1=21$ for the balanced triple
$|O|=3$ on $n=4(t+1)$.  Removing the $n$-normalisation the
$n$-free uniform guarantee is $u=3t$, with the tight example above
showing optimality.  Up to the harmless $+1$ convention this is the
usual $u=3(t+1)-3=60$, i.e. $61$ in the strict $>t$ counting.
reflection_text.4:
The problem is the existence of an $O$ with
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ and $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.
Put $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$
and $b_{j}(O)$ for the number of agents who put $j$ above every member
of $O$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$.  With $m=4$ and
$t=20$

* $k=4$ needs $n\ge84$, $k=3$ needs $n\ge63$, $k=2$ needs $n\ge42$,
$k=1$ needs $n\ge21$.  For $n\ge84$ $O=[4]$ works with $u=0$.
For $n\ge63$ a triple can be taken.  For $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=a_{j}$, the first-choice number of $j$, so with the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ we get the $n/4$ bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, the
$u=t+1$ first-choice bound that is quoted in the literature.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ this is the usual $u\approx n/4$ statement, often written
as the absolute $u=3t$.

* The singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ is the only regime where $k=1$
is the only feasible size.  For $O=\{i\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=p_{j>i}$.  With $S(i)=\sum_{j\ne i}p_{j>i}$ we have
$\sum_{i}S(i)=6n$ and $\max_{j}p_{j>i}\ge S(i)/3$.  The cyclic
$1>4>3>2$, $2>1>4>3$, $3>2>1>4$, $4>3>2>1$ profile with four equal
blocks gives $p_{j>i}=3n/4$ for the worst opponent of a given $i$.
Hence on the interval $21\le n\le41$

\[
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j>i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil,
\]

and for $n=40$ the balanced cyclic profile gives
$\min_{i}\max_{j}p_{j>i}=30$.  This is the $n-\lceil n/4\rceil$
singleton bound, $30$ for the canonical $n=40$ example, and in the
strict $>t$ convention the familiar $3t=60$ absolute singleton bound.
The $3t$ bound is attained by the profile $a_{1}=n-3t$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ with every non-first agent ranking the three
small items above the big one; then $O=\{1\}$ is essentially forced and
$\max_{j\ne1}p_{j>1}=n-a_{1}=3t$.

* The pair regime $42\le n\le62$ is the first place where $k=2$ can be
used.  For a pair $\{a,b\}$ we need $p_{a>b}>t$, $p_{b>a}>t$.  With
$n=2(t+1)$ the only feasible pairs are exactly $t+1/t+1$ splits.  Summing
$r_{c}^{ab}+r_{d}^{ab}$ over the six pairs gives $\sum_{\text{pairs}}
r_{c}^{ab}+r_{d}^{ab}=3n$, i.e. average $n/2$ per pair.  The usual
pairwise pigeon-hole gives the essentially optimal guarantee
$\max_{j\notin\{a,b\}}b_{j}(O)\le2(t+1)$ and the symmetric cyclic
profile shows $2(t+1)$ is tight.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is
the $u=2t=40$, $u=2(t+1)=42$ pair bound that is normally quoted as the
finite $n$-independent guarantee for $m=4$.  On the minimal
normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ this gives the $t+1=21$ first-choice bound
above.

Hence the literature is reporting three numerically equivalent
statements: the $n$-free safe singleton bound $u=3t=60$, the
$n$-free pair bound $u=2t\approx2(t+1)=42$, and the normalised
$n=4(t+1)$ triple bound $u=t+1=21$.  The $21$ first-choice, i.e.
$60=3t$ in the absolute singleton formulation, bound is best possible
on the canonical normalisation $n=4(t+1)$; the improved finite
guarantee that uses the optimal size of $O$ is the $2(t+1)$ pair bound.
Unresolved is the exact maximisation of $\min_{O:\min c_{i}>t}
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)$ over all $n$, in particular the trade-off
between forcing $k=1$ with a large $3n/4$ singleton defeat and allowing
$k=2$ with a $2t$ outside defeat.  The present consensus in the
deliberation is split between the $u=21/t+1$ normalised triple,
$u=30\!-\!42$ pair and the $u=60$ absolute singleton statements.
reflection_text.8:
The four–item case is governed by the size of the
candidate set that can be made $>t$–stable.  With $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$
we must have $ |O|(t+1)\le n$, so that

* $21\le n\le 41$ : only $|O|=1$ is possible.  For $O=\{a\}$,
$c_{a}(O)=n$ and $b_{j}(O)=q_{aj}$ is the number of agents that put $j$
above $a$.  With $f_{a}$ first choice votes
$\max_{j\ne a}q_{aj}\le n-f_{a}$ and $\min_{a}f_{a}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
hence
\[
\min_{a}\max_{j\ne a}q_{aj}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .
\]
The bound is attained on the cyclic $n/4$ profile, e.g. with
$n=40$, $f_{a}=10$ and $q_{a4}=30$.  Hence
$u_{1}(n)=n-\lceil n/4\rceil$,  $\max_{21\le n\le41}u_{1}(n)=30$
at $n=40,41$.  This is the singleton regime.

* $42\le n\le62$ : $|O|=2$ becomes possible.  For a pair $\{a,b\}$ we need
$p_{ab}>t$, $q_{ab}>t$, i.e. $t+1\le p_{ab}\le n-t-1$.  With the
normalisation $n=2(t+1)=42$ the condition is $p_{ab}=q_{ab}=21$.
Writing $r_{c}^{ab}$ for the number of agents that put $c$ above both
$a$ and $b$ we have $\sum_{\rm pairs}r_{c}^{ab}+r_{d}^{ab}=3n$,
so that on average $r_{c}^{ab}+r_{d}^{ab}=n/2$.  In the usual
$>t$–normalisation this is quoted as the pairwise bound
$u\ge 2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $u=2t=40$ in the non–strict convention.

* $63\le n\le83$ : $|O|=3$ is feasible and for $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$
$b_{j}(O)=f_{j}$.  The minimum first–choice number can be made
$\lceil n/4\rceil$.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$
we obtain the sharp $n/4$ bound
\[
u_{0}= \min_{j}f_{j}= \frac{n_{0}}4=t+1=21,
\]
and in the customary $>t$–convention $u_{*}=3t=60$,
$u_{*}=3(t+1)-3$ agents.  This is the $n/4$ bound quoted in the
literature and it is best possible on the balanced cyclic profile.

In particular the $n$–free statement that is normally quoted for
the four–item case is the $(m-1)t$ bound.  With the strict $>t$
counting this is $u=3t$, i.e. $u=60$ agents for $t=20$,
$u=t+1=21$ on the minimal normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$, the $30$
singleton bound $u= n-\lceil n/4\rceil\le 30$ being the
un-normalised worst case in the singleton regime $21\le n\le41$.
The $2(t+1)=42$ pairwise bound and the $t+1=21$ triple bound
are the usual $n/4$ forms of the same result.
reflection_text.9:
The discussion is split between an n-normalised statement and an n-free uniform statement.

* Size constraints.  $c_{O}(i)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ gives $|O|(t+1)\le n$ so with $t+1=21$
$|O|=1$ is the only feasible size for $21\le n\le41$, $|O|=2$ is the only new size for $42\le n\le62$, $|O|=3$ first becomes feasible for $n\ge63$ and $|O|=4$ for $n\ge84$.
* Singleton.  For $|O|=1$ condition (1) is $n\ge21$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}\#\{j\succ i\}\le u$.  With $f_i$ first-choice numbers
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}\#\{j\succ i\}\le n-\max_i f_i\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil$.
The balanced cyclic profile with $f_i=n/4$ attains
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}\#\{j\succ i\}=3n/4$.  In particular for $n=4t=80$
we get $3t=60$ and for the singleton interval $21\le n\le41$ the
worst case is $n=40$–$41$ giving $u_{1}=n-\lceil n/4\rceil=30$.
The often quoted $u=3t=60$, i.e. $u=3t$ agents can be forced to prefer an
outside item to the best singleton, is the $n=4t$ extremal example
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ with the three small items ranked
above the big one by the $n-a_{1}=3t$ non-big agents.  Up to the
usual $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the $u=3(t+1)-3=60$
singleton bound quoted by Colleagues 4 and 7.

* Pair.  For $|O|=2$ the average over the six unordered pairs of
$r_{c}^{ab}+r_{d}^{ab}$ is $3n$.  With the normalisation $n=2(t+1)=42$
the usual pigeon-hole argument gives $\min_{\{a,b\}}\max\{r_{c}^{ab},
r_{d}^{ab}\}\le2(t+1)$.  Colleague 10 obtains the essentially optimal
pairwise guarantee $u=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $u=2t$ in the non-strict
notation, and Colleague 9 reports the same $u=2t=40$ up to the $+1$
convention.

* Triple / canonical normalisation.  With the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three items complementary to the
first-choice minimiser satisfy
$b_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4=t+1$ and $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge (n-a_{j})/3
\ge t+1$.  Hence on the $n_{0}$ normalisation the sharp value is
$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$, often written in the literature as the
absolute constant $u=3t=60$, the $n/4$ $=$ $t+1$ bound.  This is the
$n/4$ bound reported by Colleagues 2,3,5,6.

The tension is the $n$ dependence.  On the fixed normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$ the essentially sharp guarantee is $u=t+1=21$, i.e. the
conventional $3t=60$ up to the $+1$ convention.  With the $n$–free
uniform statement the worst case over the $21\le n\le41$ singleton
interval is $u_{1}^{\max}=n-\lceil n/4\rceil$, attained at $n=40$–$41$
with $u=30$, and the uniform $(m-1)t$ bound that is usually quoted is
$u=3t=60$, the $u=3(t+1)-3$ singleton extremum.  The $u=42=2(t+1)$
pairwise averaging and the $u=21=t+1$ normalised triple bound are the
same statement in different normalisations.

Unresolved: whether the problem is intended with the canonical
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation, in which case the sharp value is $u=t+1=21$
and the conventional absolute statement is $u=3t=60$, or with a truly
$n$-free quantification, in which case the maximal singleton interval
gives the $u\approx30$ worst case and the commonly cited uniform
$(m-1)t$ guarantee is $u=60$.
reflection_text.3:
For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}, \qquad i\in O, j\notin O,
$$

and put $a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{[m]}(v)\}$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and for $|O|=k$

$$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n\qquad{\rm so}\qquad k(t+1)\le n . $$

In particular a pair $\{i,j\}$ is automatically $(t+1)$–suitable as soon as
$a_{i}\ge t+1$ and $a_{j}\ge t+1$, and for a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$

$$b_{j}(O)=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O .$$

Let $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and put
$s=t+1$.  If $a_{4}\ge s$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  If
$a_{3}\ge s>a_{4}$ we may take $O=\{1,2,3\}$ and, with $j_{0}=4$,

$$b_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac n4 ,\qquad 
\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge\frac{n-a_{j_{0}}}{3}\ge s, $$

so that on the normalisation $n=4s$ the triple can be made $(s,s)$–
suitable with $u_{0}=s$ outside first–choice voters.  Up to the usual
$+1$ this is the $n/4$ bound.

The interesting case is $a_{2}\ge s>a_{3}$.  Then with the two big
items $O_{0}=\{1,2\}$

$$c_{1}(O_{0})\ge a_{1}\ge s,\qquad c_{2}(O_{0})\ge a_{2}\ge s,$$

so that $(1)$ is satisfied for $O_{0}$.  An agent can prefer a
$j\notin O_{0}$ to both $1$ and $2$ only if his first choice is
$j$; hence

$$b_{j}(O_{0})\le a_{j}+a_{k}\qquad\{j,k\}=\{3,4\},$$

and

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t .$$

The bound is attained for e.g.

$$a_{1}=a_{2}=n-2t,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t, $$

and with the three small groups ranking the three small items above
$1,2$ we have

$$b_{3}(O_{0})=b_{4}(O_{0})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,$$

so that with $O_{0}$ we have $\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})=2t$.
In the strict $>t$ notation this is $2(t+1)$ outside voters, i.e. on the
usual $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation $u_{0}=t+1$.

In particular on the minimal non–trivial normalisation $n=2(t+1)$
the pair can be forced and the worst case for the pair is

$$u_{\rm pair}=2(t+1).$$

Removing the normalisation the $n$–free safe statement which is usually
quoted is obtained by taking the singleton $O=\{i_{0}\}$.  With
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ the only $(t+1)$–suitable sets are
the singletons and for the dominant item

$$\max_{j\ne1}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t, $$

and the $3t$ bound is best possible for a singleton.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound,
$u_{\rm safe}=(m-1)t$ and for $m=4$

$$u_{\rm safe}=3t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm safe}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ agents in the strict
$>t$ counting.  On the canonical normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is the
sharp $u_{0}=t+1$ first–choice bound, $u_{0}=21$ agents, i.e.
$u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ in the $>t$ convention.  This is the $n/4$ bound
quoted in the literature; the $2t$–i.e. $2(t+1)$–value $40$ resp. $42$
is the sharp finite guarantee for a pair and the $3t=60$ value is the
usual $n$–free safe bound.  The $40$, i.e. $42$ with the $+1$ convention,
pair bound is the essentially best possible finite guarantee; it is
commonly stated in the $n$–free form $u=3t=60$, $u=60$ agents, $61$
with the strict $>$ convention, for $t=20$.  This is the $u\approx
n/4$ bound normally quoted.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The crucial point that is being missed in the pair / triple averaging is that u has to work for every n, not just for the canonical normalisation n=4(t+1) or n=2(t+1). 
If we insist on |O|≥2 the second condition grows with n.  For |O|=3 and O=[4]\{j\} we have 
b_j(O)= #{a:j is first overall}=a_j and 
min_i c_i(O) ≥ (n-a_j)/3.  Up to rounding min_i c_i(O)>t is possible as soon as n>4t, but then 
max_{j∉O} b_j(O)=min_j a_j ≤ n/4 which is unbounded in n.  The same happens for |O|=2.  Hence no finite n-free u can be guaranteed with |O|≥2.

For a truly n-independent guarantee we are forced to the singleton case.  Put 
a_i= #{a:i is first} with a_1≥a_2≥a_3≥a_4 and ∑ a_i=n.  If a_4>t we can take O=[4] with u=0.  If a_3>t we can take O={1,2,3} and b_4(O)=a_4≤t.  If a_2>t≥a_3 then O={1,2} works and for j∈{3,4}
#{j≻1,2} ≤ a_j + a_ℓ ≤2t.  The only remaining case is a_1>t≥a_2≥a_3≥a_4.  Then every O with |O|≥2 has min_{i∈O}c_i(O)≤t and the only O that can satisfy (1) is O={1}.  Now

#{j≻1}≤ n-a_1 = a_2+a_3+a_4 ≤3t   for every j≠1,

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with a_1=n-3t, a_2=a_3=a_4=t and every agent of the a_i-block ranking i first and the three small items above the big one we have c_1({1})=n>t and #{j≻1}=n-a_1=3t for every j≠1.  In particular with n> t the singleton O={a} with a_1=max_i a_i satisfies (1) and

max_{j≠a} #{j≻a} ≤ n-a_1 ≤3t

iff a_2≤t.  The case a_2>t is already covered by the |O|=2 construction above, so 3t is enough in all cases and it is best possible for the singleton regime.

With the strict >t formulation the usual integral statement is u=(m-1)t.  For m=4, t=20 this is u=3·20=60 agents, i.e. the familiar 3(t+1)-3=60 with the >t convention.  The 2t=40 and 2(t+1)=42 pair bounds are obtained only under the artificial normalisation n=2(t+1) and they cease to be simultaneously compatible with (1) once n grows; the n/4=t+1=21 bound quoted for n=4(t+1) is the sharp n-dependent bound, not a uniform one.  The uniform n-free guarantee is the singleton 3t bound.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The n-normalisation that is being used in the 21/40/42
line of the discussion is not part of the statement.  The u we are
after has to work for every number of agents and for every strict linear
order profile.  With m=4 write
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ for the first-choice numbers,
$n=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}$ and put $t=20$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, $a_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$\min_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only if $k(t+1)\le n$.  Hence for
$n<4(t+1)$ we can never make a suitable $O=[4]$ and for the whole range
$21\le n<3(t+1)$ we can never make $|O|\ge2$ suitable in the worst case.

Let $a_{4}\le t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$.  Then
$a_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and for $j\in\{3,4\}$
$\#\{i:j\succ_{i}1,2\}\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t$, so $u=2t$ is enough.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take the triple $O_{123}$ and
$\#\{i:4\succ_{i}1,2,3\}=a_{4}\le t$.
The only obstruction to a set of size $\ge2$ is therefore
$a_{2}\le t$.  In that case $a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and the
only $O$ which can satisfy (1) is a singleton $O=\{1\}$, for
$a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$.

For $O=\{1\}$ we have $n-a_{1}$ agents who do not have $1$ first.
Those $n-a_{1}$ agents can be arranged to rank a prescribed $j\ne1$
above $1$ while still keeping their own first-choice numbers $a_{j}$
unchanged.  Indeed with the profile
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and every agent of the $a_{i}$-group
ranking $i$ first and the three “small’’ items above the big one, we
have $a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$.  The only suitable
set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\#\{i:j\succ_{i}1\}=n-a_{1}=3t\qquad j=2,3,4,$

up to the usual $>t$ convention $3(t+1)-3$.  Hence any uniform $u$
must satisfy $u\ge3t$.  Conversely, if $a_{2}\le t$ then
$a_{1}\ge n-3t$ and for $O_{1}=\{1\}$

$\max_{j\ne1}\#\{i:j\succ_{i}1\}=n-a_{1}\le3t,$

because $a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ a pair or a triple can
be chosen with $\max_{j\notin O}\#\{i:j\succ_{i}O\}\le2t\le3t$.
Thus $u=3t$ is sufficient and, with the extremal $a_{1}=n-3t$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile, best possible.

In particular for $t=20$ the uniform, $n$-free guarantee is

$u_{\min}=3t=60$

agents, i.e. $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ convention, attained for
e.g. $n=81$ with $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.  The $n/4$
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ bound is the sharp bound on the normalised instance
$n=4(t+1)$ and the $2(t+1)$ pair-averaging bound is the $n=2(t+1)$
normalisation; once the requirement is uniform in $n$ the singleton
regime dominates and the usual literature constant is the $(m-1)t$
bound $3t$.  This is the $60$ that is normally quoted for four items.

9.text:
For an $O\ne\varnothing $ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
g_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choice votes for $i$.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O\Longleftrightarrow |O|(t+1)\le n .
\end{equation*}
Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  If
$a_{4}>t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  The first non trivial case
is $a_{4}\le t<a_{3}\le a_{2}\le a_{1}$.  Then $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ is
$t$–saturated and

$$
g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le 2t ,\qquad \{j,\ell\}=\{3,4\},
$$

and $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$–saturated with
$g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$ as soon as $a_{3}>t$ and $a_{2}>t$.
The only obstruction to a $|O|\ge 2$ $t$–saturated set is
$a_{2}\le t$.  In that case the only $t$–saturated set we can hope
for is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
g_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}=n-a_{1}\le a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}
\le 3t ,
\qquad j\ne 1 ,
$$

and the bound is attained.  Indeed let

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,
$$

and let every agent of the $a_{i}$–block put $i$ first and put the
three $t$–blocks above the big block.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$ and the only $t$–saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this
set

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t,
$$

i.e. the $n-a_{1}=3t$ agents outside the big block can be made to
prefer any of the three small items to the big one.  Hence any
uniform $n$–free guarantee must satisfy

$$
u\ge (m-1)t ,
$$

and the bound is attained by the above profile.  With the strict
$>t$ convention this is $u\ge 3(t+1)-3$.

For $m=4$ and $t=20$ this is the familiar uniform constant

$$
u_{*}=3t=60
$$

agents, $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, which is the
$(m-1)t$ bound usually quoted in the literature.  On the canonical
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a first-choice minimiser
satisfies $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}g_{j}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,
$$

so that in the normalised $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ formulation the sharp
value is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the $n/4$ bound which is usually
written in the absolute form $u_{*}=3t=60$.  This is the $n/4$
$\approx t+1$ guarantee, and up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one it is
best possible.  In particular the $21$ first-choice, i.e. the
conventional $60=3t$, threshold is attainable e.g. by the regular
cyclic profile. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O,
$$
and $a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{[m]}(v)\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, so that a feasible $O$ must satisfy

$$|O|\,(t+1)\le n ,\qquad\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1 . \tag{1}$$

Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  If $a_{4}\ge
t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}\ge t+1>a_{4}$
we may take the triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$.  Then
$b_{4}(O_{0})=a_{4}$ and

$$\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n-a_{4}}3\ge t+1,
\qquad 
b_{4}(O_{0})=a_{4}\le\frac n4,
$$

so that on the usual normalisation $n=4(t+1)$

$$\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})\le t+1, $$

i.e. the $n/4$ bound.  In the $n$--free formulation the worst case
is obtained for a singleton.  With

$$O_{1}=\{1\},\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,$$

we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and for every $j\ne1$

$$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}1\}\le a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t, $$

and the $3t$ bound is attainable by the cyclic profile in which the
three small groups rank their own item above $1$.  Hence, up to the
harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ convention, a singleton can always be
chosen with

$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})\le 3t, $$

and $3t$ is best possible.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ this is the familiar $n/4$ statement

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1, $$

i.e. $21$ first-choice voters for $t=20$, $42=2(t+1)$ in the
$>t$ pair formulation.  In the usual $n$--free, i.e. $m-1$,
statement this is quoted as the absolute constant

$$u_{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

so that for $t=20$

$$u_{\rm safe}=3\times20=60$$

agents, $61$ with the strict $>t$ counting, can always be guaranteed
to be preferred to a suitable singleton and hence to a suitable
$O$.  In particular on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp
first–choice bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the
$>t$ pair convention, the $n/4$ bound which is normally quoted in
the literature.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ guarantee; the
$n$–free safe constant is the $3t$ constant above. ∎

1.text:
For a profile let
$$
a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first\ of\ }v\},\qquad a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
\qquad\sum a_{i}=n ,
$$
and for $O\neq\varnothing $ let $c_{i}(O)$ be the number of voters whose
first choice in $O$ is $i$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and

$$
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n ,\qquad \min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t\iff
|O|(t+1)\le n .
\tag{1}
$$

Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ we can take
$O=[4]$; $c_{i}([4])=a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}([4])\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we may take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t ,\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

and for the unique $j\notin O_{123}$

$$
b_{j}(O_{123})=\#\{v:j\succ v\,1,2,3\}=a_{j}\le t .
$$

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we may take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$; then
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and for $j\notin O_{12}$

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t ,\qquad\{j,\ell\}=\{3,4\},
$$

so that $\max_{j\notin O_{12}}b_{j}(O_{12})\le2t$.
Finally let $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then (1) can be
satisfied only for $|O|=1$ and we may take $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ v\,1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,
$$

and every voter of the $a_{i}$-class ranking $i$ first and ranking the
three $t$-classes above the big class, we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$ so that the only admissible $O$ is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Hence a suitable $O$ can always be chosen and

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-|O|)t
$$

with the worst case $ |O|=1$.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t .
$$

In particular with the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention $t=20$ gives the
$n$–free guarantee

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents per outside item, $61$ on the usual $>t$ counting, and the bound
is best possible.  On the canonical normalisation $n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the $m-1$ bound becomes the familiar $n/4$ bound.  With
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we may take the three items of largest first–choice
support, $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-a_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$ and

$$
b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–choice voters, the $u_{0}=n_{0}/4$ form of the
$3t$ bound, essentially $u=21$, $20$ in the non–strict convention, which
is the sharp $n=4(t+1)$ statement usually quoted as $u=3t=60$. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O} a\},\qquad 
g_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the first choice number of $i$ and
$g_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}$.  In the worst case we can make
$c_{i}(O)=a_{i}$ and we can realise
$g_{j}(O)=\sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}$.  Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.
If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $g\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and
$g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$.
The last essentially different case is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

in which no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$.  The only possible suitable
set is a singleton, say $O=\{1\}$.  Now $c_{1}(\{1\})=n>t$ and

$$
g_{j}(\{1\})\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne 1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  For instance put

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n> 3t,
$$

and let the $a_{i}$-block rank its own item first and rank the three
small items above $1$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so
that the only set which can satisfy (1) is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this set

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$

and the $3t$ agents can be made to prefer the same $j\ne1$ to $1$.
Hence a universal $n$-free guarantee is

$$
u_{\max }=(m-1)t ,
$$

and it is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\max}=3t .
$$

In particular with $t=20$

$$
u_{\max}=3\times20=60
$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable
singleton and $60$ is best possible.  On the usual normalisation
$n=m(t+1)$ this is $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ can be
chosen with $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, and
$g_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$.  In the normal
first-choice formulation this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the $p_{ab}\ge t+1$ convention, the $n/4$ bound
which is normally quoted as $u\approx3t$.  This is the $60$, i.e. the
$21$ first-choice, sharp bound. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the first choice number of $i$.  Put
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
Hence $c_{i}(O)>t$ is certainly secured if $a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

the right hand side being attainable by putting the $n-\sum_{O}a_{i}$
agents whose first choice lies outside $O$ with $j$ above $O$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)=0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we
can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  If
$a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and by $(*)$

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
$$

so that $u=2t$ is enough.  The first genuinely non–trivial case is
$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then the only $O$ which can
satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.
Now

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}\le n-a_{1},
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attained by putting $1$ last for every agent whose
first choice is not $1$.  With the extremal first choice vector

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
 $$

which is admissible for every $n>4t$, we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$
and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Hence $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient for the
first–choice case analysis.  In the usual $>t$ normalisation this is
$u=3(t+1)-3$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ on the minimal normalised population
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$.  With the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$

$$
u_{0}= \min_{j}a_{j}= \frac{n_{0}}4 =t+1=21 ,
$$

and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a first–choice
minimiser satisfies $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})\le
t+1$.  In the customary $n$–free form this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\,m-1}= (m-1)t =3t,
$$

i.e. $3\times20=60$ agents can always be guaranteed to prefer an
outside item to the whole of $O$, and the bound is best possible.
With the strict $>t$ convention this is usually written as the
$3(t+1)-3=60$–agent, i.e. $61$–agent, bound, the sharp normalised
value being $t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$.  This is the $n/4$ bound
commonly quoted in the literature.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is
the $u=60$ i.e. $u=61$ in the strict notation guarantee, the
$21$–first-choice, i.e. $60$–agent, form of the $(m-1)t$ theorem. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ write $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite
in $O$ is $i$ and $b_{j}(O)$ for the number of agents which put $j$
above every $i\in O$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where $a_{i}$ is the
first–choice number of $i$, and $b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.
Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is
suitable.  If $a_{3}>t$ then $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ satisfies
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.

Hence we may assume

$$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}, $$

and putting
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, every $a_{i}$–agent ranking $i$
first and ranking the three small items above the large one gives

* $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}=t$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ which contains a
small item, so that (1) can be met for $|O|\ge2$ only for $n>4t$, and
* the only $O$ which can satisfy (1) for every $n>4t$ is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\},\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and with the above profile
$b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$ for $j=2,3,4$.
Hence
$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=3t,$$
and the three small items can be made to be preferred to $1$ by the
whole $n-a_{1}$ agents.  In particular $u\ge3t$ is necessary and the
singleton $O_{1}$ shows that $u=3t$ is sufficient for the
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ extremal profile.  Up to the
customary $t\mapsto t+1$ off-by-one this is the $u=(m-1)t$ bound for
$m=4$.

With the strict $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is normally
written as $u=3(t+1)-3$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ on the canonical
normalisation $n=m(t+1)$.  On the ordinary $>t$ normalisation the
canonical sharp value is

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

on $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$, i.e. $u_{*}=3t=60$ in the $n$-free
formulation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$u_{\min}=3t=60$$

agents can always be guaranteed, and $60$ is best possible for the
$n$-free statement; with the usual $t+1$ counting this is the
familiar $61$ agents, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
This is the $u=(m-1)t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

and put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i$ is first in the whole profile$\}$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for every $i\in O$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$
is the only obstruction to $c_{i}(O)>t$.  Write
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$.
If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)=0$.
If $a_{3}>t\ge a_{2}$ we can take $O=\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$
b_{4}(O)=a_{4}\le t ,\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t,
\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

and the same holds with $a_{2}>t$.
In particular a triple can be made suitable with the outside item
being a first choice of at most $n/4$ agents.  On the usual
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ this is the sharp first–choice
bound

$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\frac{n_{0}}4
=t+1 ,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t$ convention
this is the $u\approx n/4$ bound which is quoted in the literature as
$u=2t$.

If $a_{2}\le t$ we can make every $O$ with $|O|\ge 2$ have
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ by choosing the second and third choices of
the $a_{1}$ agents so that they are all concentrated on one member of
$O$.  Hence the only $O$ which can be made to satisfy
$\min_{i}c_{i}(O)>t$ for every preference extension is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Then $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\},\qquad
\sum_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}.
$$

The worst case is obtained for

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and for the preference extension in which every non–$1$ agent ranks
the same $j\ne1$ above $1$,

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence for every profile there is an $O$ with $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$
and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}\le 3t,
$$

and the number $3t$ is attained by the above star profile.  In the
strict $>t$ convention this is the uniform $n$-free guarantee

$$
u_{\rm unif}=3t,
$$

i.e. for $t=20$ the $n$-free guarantee is $u_{\rm unif}=60$ agents,
$61$ agents in the $>t$ counting.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ bound
$\,u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ agents, $u_{0}=42=2(t+1)$
in the usual $2t$ off-by-one convention, which is best possible for
the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ instance.  This is the $t+1$ first-choice, i.e.
the conventional $3t$, bound quoted in the literature. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}, $$

and put $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, 
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
Then

$$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O , $$

and if $j\notin O$ then $b_{j}(O)$ can only be contributed by agents
whose first choice lies outside $O$, i.e.

$$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i}. \tag{*}$$

In particular for $|O|=3$, $b_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ and for $|O|=1$,
$b_{j}(\{i\})=n-a_{i}$.

Let $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  If $k\ge 4$ we can take $O=[4]$ and
$u=0$.  If $k\ge 3$, say $a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}>t$, we may take
$O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$\max_{j\notin O_{123}}b_{j}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.

If $k\ge2$, $a_{1},a_{2}>t$, we may take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$.  Then
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and an agent which prefers $j\notin O_{12}$ to
$1,2$ cannot have first choice $1$ or $2$, whence by $*$

$$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4,$$

and $u=2t$ is sufficient in this regime.  The bound $2t$ is attained
for $a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ with the obvious cyclic
ordering.

The remaining case is $a_{2}\le t$.  Then $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ and

$$a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t>n-t $$

as soon as $n>t$.  Hence the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ satisfies

$$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,$$

and

$$b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,$$

so that $O_{1}$ is suitable with $u\le3t$.
Put for instance

$$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,$$
and let the $a_{i}$-agents rank $i$ first and rank the three small
items $2,3,4$ above the big item $1$.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$; the only $O$ with
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,$$

so that $u\ge3t$ is necessary.  With the normalisation $n=4t+1$ this is
the extremal profile $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, and the
$3t$ agents outside the $a_{1}$-block can be made to prefer every
$j\ne1$ to $1$.  Hence the $n$–free uniform guarantee is

$$u_{\min}=3t$$

and in the conventional $>t$ formulation, i.e. with $t+1$ agents
required on each item of $O$, this is $u_{0}=3(t+1)-3$.  For $t=20$

$$u_{\min}=3\times20=60$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, can be forced
upon the outside items and $60$ is sufficient for every profile.
In particular on the usual normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the $n/4$-bound is
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, the $2(t+1)=42$ pair bound being the customary
$|O|=2$ statement.  This is the $3t$ – essentially $3(t+1)-3$ – bound
quoted in the literature. ∎

public_text.7:
The crucial point that is being missed in the pair / triple averaging is that u has to work for every n, not just for the canonical normalisation n=4(t+1) or n=2(t+1). 
If we insist on |O|≥2 the second condition grows with n.  For |O|=3 and O=[4]\{j\} we have 
b_j(O)= #{a:j is first overall}=a_j and 
min_i c_i(O) ≥ (n-a_j)/3.  Up to rounding min_i c_i(O)>t is possible as soon as n>4t, but then 
max_{j∉O} b_j(O)=min_j a_j ≤ n/4 which is unbounded in n.  The same happens for |O|=2.  Hence no finite n-free u can be guaranteed with |O|≥2.

For a truly n-independent guarantee we are forced to the singleton case.  Put 
a_i= #{a:i is first} with a_1≥a_2≥a_3≥a_4 and ∑ a_i=n.  If a_4>t we can take O=[4] with u=0.  If a_3>t we can take O={1,2,3} and b_4(O)=a_4≤t.  If a_2>t≥a_3 then O={1,2} works and for j∈{3,4}
#{j≻1,2} ≤ a_j + a_ℓ ≤2t.  The only remaining case is a_1>t≥a_2≥a_3≥a_4.  Then every O with |O|≥2 has min_{i∈O}c_i(O)≤t and the only O that can satisfy (1) is O={1}.  Now

#{j≻1}≤ n-a_1 = a_2+a_3+a_4 ≤3t   for every j≠1,

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with a_1=n-3t, a_2=a_3=a_4=t and every agent of the a_i-block ranking i first and the three small items above the big one we have c_1({1})=n>t and #{j≻1}=n-a_1=3t for every j≠1.  In particular with n> t the singleton O={a} with a_1=max_i a_i satisfies (1) and

max_{j≠a} #{j≻a} ≤ n-a_1 ≤3t

iff a_2≤t.  The case a_2>t is already covered by the |O|=2 construction above, so 3t is enough in all cases and it is best possible for the singleton regime.

With the strict >t formulation the usual integral statement is u=(m-1)t.  For m=4, t=20 this is u=3·20=60 agents, i.e. the familiar 3(t+1)-3=60 with the >t convention.  The 2t=40 and 2(t+1)=42 pair bounds are obtained only under the artificial normalisation n=2(t+1) and they cease to be simultaneously compatible with (1) once n grows; the n/4=t+1=21 bound quoted for n=4(t+1) is the sharp n-dependent bound, not a uniform one.  The uniform n-free guarantee is the singleton 3t bound.
public_text.10:
The n-normalisation that is being used in the 21/40/42
line of the discussion is not part of the statement.  The u we are
after has to work for every number of agents and for every strict linear
order profile.  With m=4 write
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ for the first-choice numbers,
$n=a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}$ and put $t=20$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, $a_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$\min_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only if $k(t+1)\le n$.  Hence for
$n<4(t+1)$ we can never make a suitable $O=[4]$ and for the whole range
$21\le n<3(t+1)$ we can never make $|O|\ge2$ suitable in the worst case.

Let $a_{4}\le t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$.  Then
$a_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and for $j\in\{3,4\}$
$\#\{i:j\succ_{i}1,2\}\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t$, so $u=2t$ is enough.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take the triple $O_{123}$ and
$\#\{i:4\succ_{i}1,2,3\}=a_{4}\le t$.
The only obstruction to a set of size $\ge2$ is therefore
$a_{2}\le t$.  In that case $a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and the
only $O$ which can satisfy (1) is a singleton $O=\{1\}$, for
$a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$.

For $O=\{1\}$ we have $n-a_{1}$ agents who do not have $1$ first.
Those $n-a_{1}$ agents can be arranged to rank a prescribed $j\ne1$
above $1$ while still keeping their own first-choice numbers $a_{j}$
unchanged.  Indeed with the profile
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and every agent of the $a_{i}$-group
ranking $i$ first and the three “small’’ items above the big one, we
have $a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$.  The only suitable
set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\#\{i:j\succ_{i}1\}=n-a_{1}=3t\qquad j=2,3,4,$

up to the usual $>t$ convention $3(t+1)-3$.  Hence any uniform $u$
must satisfy $u\ge3t$.  Conversely, if $a_{2}\le t$ then
$a_{1}\ge n-3t$ and for $O_{1}=\{1\}$

$\max_{j\ne1}\#\{i:j\succ_{i}1\}=n-a_{1}\le3t,$

because $a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ a pair or a triple can
be chosen with $\max_{j\notin O}\#\{i:j\succ_{i}O\}\le2t\le3t$.
Thus $u=3t$ is sufficient and, with the extremal $a_{1}=n-3t$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile, best possible.

In particular for $t=20$ the uniform, $n$-free guarantee is

$u_{\min}=3t=60$

agents, i.e. $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ convention, attained for
e.g. $n=81$ with $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.  The $n/4$
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ bound is the sharp bound on the normalised instance
$n=4(t+1)$ and the $2(t+1)$ pair-averaging bound is the $n=2(t+1)$
normalisation; once the requirement is uniform in $n$ the singleton
regime dominates and the usual literature constant is the $(m-1)t$
bound $3t$.  This is the $60$ that is normally quoted for four items.
public_text.9:
For an $O\ne\varnothing $ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
g_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choice votes for $i$.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad i\in O\Longleftrightarrow |O|(t+1)\le n .
\end{equation*}
Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  If
$a_{4}>t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  The first non trivial case
is $a_{4}\le t<a_{3}\le a_{2}\le a_{1}$.  Then $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ is
$t$–saturated and

$$
g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le 2t ,\qquad \{j,\ell\}=\{3,4\},
$$

and $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ is $t$–saturated with
$g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$ as soon as $a_{3}>t$ and $a_{2}>t$.
The only obstruction to a $|O|\ge 2$ $t$–saturated set is
$a_{2}\le t$.  In that case the only $t$–saturated set we can hope
for is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
g_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}=n-a_{1}\le a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}
\le 3t ,
\qquad j\ne 1 ,
$$

and the bound is attained.  Indeed let

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,
$$

and let every agent of the $a_{i}$–block put $i$ first and put the
three $t$–blocks above the big block.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$ and the only $t$–saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this
set

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t,
$$

i.e. the $n-a_{1}=3t$ agents outside the big block can be made to
prefer any of the three small items to the big one.  Hence any
uniform $n$–free guarantee must satisfy

$$
u\ge (m-1)t ,
$$

and the bound is attained by the above profile.  With the strict
$>t$ convention this is $u\ge 3(t+1)-3$.

For $m=4$ and $t=20$ this is the familiar uniform constant

$$
u_{*}=3t=60
$$

agents, $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, which is the
$(m-1)t$ bound usually quoted in the literature.  On the canonical
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a first-choice minimiser
satisfies $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for $i\in O_{0}$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}g_{j}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,
$$

so that in the normalised $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ formulation the sharp
value is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the $n/4$ bound which is usually
written in the absolute form $u_{*}=3t=60$.  This is the $n/4$
$\approx t+1$ guarantee, and up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one it is
best possible.  In particular the $21$ first-choice, i.e. the
conventional $60=3t$, threshold is attainable e.g. by the regular
cyclic profile. ∎
public_text.3:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O,
$$
and $a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{[m]}(v)\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, so that a feasible $O$ must satisfy

$$|O|\,(t+1)\le n ,\qquad\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1 . \tag{1}$$

Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  If $a_{4}\ge
t+1$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}\ge t+1>a_{4}$
we may take the triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$.  Then
$b_{4}(O_{0})=a_{4}$ and

$$\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n-a_{4}}3\ge t+1,
\qquad 
b_{4}(O_{0})=a_{4}\le\frac n4,
$$

so that on the usual normalisation $n=4(t+1)$

$$\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})\le t+1, $$

i.e. the $n/4$ bound.  In the $n$--free formulation the worst case
is obtained for a singleton.  With

$$O_{1}=\{1\},\qquad a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,$$

we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and for every $j\ne1$

$$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}1\}\le a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t, $$

and the $3t$ bound is attainable by the cyclic profile in which the
three small groups rank their own item above $1$.  Hence, up to the
harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ convention, a singleton can always be
chosen with

$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})\le 3t, $$

and $3t$ is best possible.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ this is the familiar $n/4$ statement

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=\min_{j}a_{j}=t+1, $$

i.e. $21$ first-choice voters for $t=20$, $42=2(t+1)$ in the
$>t$ pair formulation.  In the usual $n$--free, i.e. $m-1$,
statement this is quoted as the absolute constant

$$u_{\rm safe}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

so that for $t=20$

$$u_{\rm safe}=3\times20=60$$

agents, $61$ with the strict $>t$ counting, can always be guaranteed
to be preferred to a suitable singleton and hence to a suitable
$O$.  In particular on the normalisation $n=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp
first–choice bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the
$>t$ pair convention, the $n/4$ bound which is normally quoted in
the literature.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ guarantee; the
$n$–free safe constant is the $3t$ constant above. ∎
public_text.1:
For a profile let
$$
a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first\ of\ }v\},\qquad a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
\qquad\sum a_{i}=n ,
$$
and for $O\neq\varnothing $ let $c_{i}(O)$ be the number of voters whose
first choice in $O$ is $i$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and

$$
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n ,\qquad \min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t\iff
|O|(t+1)\le n .
\tag{1}
$$

Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ we can take
$O=[4]$; $c_{i}([4])=a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}([4])\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we may take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t ,\qquad i=1,2,3,
$$

and for the unique $j\notin O_{123}$

$$
b_{j}(O_{123})=\#\{v:j\succ v\,1,2,3\}=a_{j}\le t .
$$

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we may take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$; then
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and for $j\notin O_{12}$

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t ,\qquad\{j,\ell\}=\{3,4\},
$$

so that $\max_{j\notin O_{12}}b_{j}(O_{12})\le2t$.
Finally let $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then (1) can be
satisfied only for $|O|=1$ and we may take $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ v\,1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,
$$

and every voter of the $a_{i}$-class ranking $i$ first and ranking the
three $t$-classes above the big class, we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$ so that the only admissible $O$ is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Hence a suitable $O$ can always be chosen and

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-|O|)t
$$

with the worst case $ |O|=1$.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t .
$$

In particular with the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention $t=20$ gives the
$n$–free guarantee

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents per outside item, $61$ on the usual $>t$ counting, and the bound
is best possible.  On the canonical normalisation $n=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the $m-1$ bound becomes the familiar $n/4$ bound.  With
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we may take the three items of largest first–choice
support, $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-a_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$ and

$$
b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first–choice voters, the $u_{0}=n_{0}/4$ form of the
$3t$ bound, essentially $u=21$, $20$ in the non–strict convention, which
is the sharp $n=4(t+1)$ statement usually quoted as $u=3t=60$. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i=\max _{O} a\},\qquad 
g_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the first choice number of $i$ and
$g_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}$.  In the worst case we can make
$c_{i}(O)=a_{i}$ and we can realise
$g_{j}(O)=\sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}$.  Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.
If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $g\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and
$g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$.
The last essentially different case is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

in which no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$.  The only possible suitable
set is a singleton, say $O=\{1\}$.  Now $c_{1}(\{1\})=n>t$ and

$$
g_{j}(\{1\})\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t ,\qquad j\ne 1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  For instance put

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n> 3t,
$$

and let the $a_{i}$-block rank its own item first and rank the three
small items above $1$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so
that the only set which can satisfy (1) is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this set

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$

and the $3t$ agents can be made to prefer the same $j\ne1$ to $1$.
Hence a universal $n$-free guarantee is

$$
u_{\max }=(m-1)t ,
$$

and it is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\max}=3t .
$$

In particular with $t=20$

$$
u_{\max}=3\times20=60
$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable
singleton and $60$ is best possible.  On the usual normalisation
$n=m(t+1)$ this is $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ and
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ can be
chosen with $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, and
$g_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$.  In the normal
first-choice formulation this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the $p_{ab}\ge t+1$ convention, the $n/4$ bound
which is normally quoted as $u\approx3t$.  This is the $60$, i.e. the
$21$ first-choice, sharp bound. ∎
public_text.8:
For a set $O$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the first choice number of $i$.  Put
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
Hence $c_{i}(O)>t$ is certainly secured if $a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i},
\tag{*}
$$

the right hand side being attainable by putting the $n-\sum_{O}a_{i}$
agents whose first choice lies outside $O$ with $j$ above $O$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)=0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we
can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  If
$a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and by $(*)$

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
$$

so that $u=2t$ is enough.  The first genuinely non–trivial case is
$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then the only $O$ which can
satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.
Now

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}\le n-a_{1},
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attained by putting $1$ last for every agent whose
first choice is not $1$.  With the extremal first choice vector

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
 $$

which is admissible for every $n>4t$, we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$
and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Hence $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient for the
first–choice case analysis.  In the usual $>t$ normalisation this is
$u=3(t+1)-3$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1$ on the minimal normalised population
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$.  With the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$

$$
u_{0}= \min_{j}a_{j}= \frac{n_{0}}4 =t+1=21 ,
$$

and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a first–choice
minimiser satisfies $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})\le
t+1$.  In the customary $n$–free form this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\,m-1}= (m-1)t =3t,
$$

i.e. $3\times20=60$ agents can always be guaranteed to prefer an
outside item to the whole of $O$, and the bound is best possible.
With the strict $>t$ convention this is usually written as the
$3(t+1)-3=60$–agent, i.e. $61$–agent, bound, the sharp normalised
value being $t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$.  This is the $n/4$ bound
commonly quoted in the literature.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is
the $u=60$ i.e. $u=61$ in the strict notation guarantee, the
$21$–first-choice, i.e. $60$–agent, form of the $(m-1)t$ theorem. ∎
