reflection_text.2:
The discussion is now essentially stable on the first-choice analysis.

Put $a_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm first}\},\;a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\;\sum a_{i}=n$
and for $O\ne\varnothing$ $c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ so that $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only
if $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  In particular $b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.

* If $a_{4}>t$ $O=[4]$ works with $u=0$.
* If $a_{3}>t$ $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ works with
$\min c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
* If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ the pair $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ works with
$\min c_{i}(O_{12})>t$ and $b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.

The obstruction is therefore $a_{2}\le t$.  Then $a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}
\ge n-3t$ and every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ meets a small item $i$ with
$c_{i}(O)=a_{i}=t$.  Hence for all $n>4t$ the only $t$-saturated set
that can be forced in the worst case is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$ with $a_{1}=\max a_{i}$.

For $O_{1}=\{1\}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and
$b_{j}(O_{1})\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$ for every $j\ne1$.
The bound is sharp.  With

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and every $a_{i}$-agent ranking $i$ first and the three small items
above the big one, we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$b_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t,\qquad j=2,3,4,$

i.e. the $n-a_{1}$ agents outside the big block can be made to prefer
any prescribed small item to $1$.  Hence a uniform $n$-free guarantee
needs $u\ge3t$ and $u=3t$ is sufficient, the usual $(m-1)t$ bound.

With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention this is quoted as
$u=3(t+1)-3$.  For $t=20$

$u_{\rm unif}=3t=60$,

$61$ in the $>t$ counting, and it is best possible for the star
profile $a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, e.g. $n=81,\;a_{1}=21$,
$a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a first-choice minimiser
satisfies $\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-a_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$
and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$.  Hence the sharp
$n$-dependent value is

$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$,

i.e. $42=2(t+1)$ in the pair formulation, the familiar $n/4$ bound.
The $21$ first-choice, $60=3t$ absolute, statement is the one
normally quoted; the $30$ and $42$ figures are the $n=2(t+1)$ and
$n=4(t+1)$ normalised versions.  No finite $n$-free $u$ exists for
$|O|\ge2$, so the singleton regime dominates the uniform problem.
reflection_text.8:
The four-item problem is controlled by the size of the set that can be made
>t-stable.  With $c_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$ we need $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Write $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ for the
first-choice numbers.

* $a_{4}>t$ : $O=[4]$ works, $u=0$.
* $a_{3}>t$ : $O_{123}$ works and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le n/4$.
* $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ : $O_{12}$ works and $b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$.
The only obstruction to $|O|\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$, i.e. $a_{1}\ge n-3t$.

In the $a_{2}\le t$ regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-stable in the
worst case.  The only feasible $O$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and
$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$.
The star profile
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, the $a_{i}$-agents ranking $i$ first
and the three $t$-blocks above the big block, makes
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and
$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t$.
Hence $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient for the
$n$-free problem.  With the strict $>t$ convention this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound, $u_{\rm unif}= (m-1)t$ and for $m=4,\;t=20$
$u_{\rm unif}=3\cdot20=60$, $61$ on the strict $t+1$ counting.

The $n$-dependent, normally quoted, statements are the normalised ones.
On $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$
with $j_{0}$ a first-choice minimiser satisfies
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$.
Hence the sharp normalised first-choice bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
i.e. $u_{0}=n/4$.  The $2(t+1)=42$ pair averaging and the $2t=40$
non-strict pair bound are the $n=2(t+1)$ normalisation of the same
phenomenon.  In the singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ the worst case is
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{j\succ i\}=n-\lceil n/4\rceil$, maximal
$30$ at $n=40,41$.

Hence there is an $n$-free uniform guarantee $u=(m-1)t=60$ which is best
possible, and the usual literature $n/4$ statement is the
normalised $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $42=2(t+1)$ in the $>t$ pair convention,
$60=3t$ in the $n$-free $(m-1)t$ form.  Colleagues 1,4,6,7,8,9 converge
on the uniform $3t$ bound; the $42/21/40$ values are the same bound
under the implicit normalisations $n=2(t+1)$ and $n=4(t+1)$.
reflection_text.6:
For a profile let
$a_{i}$ be the number of first choice votes for $i$, 
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$ and let
$c_{i}(O)$ be the number of voters for whom $i$ is the best member of
$O$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n ,
\tag{1}
$$

and for $j\notin O$ an agent can have $j\succ_{a}O$ only if his first
choice lies in $[m]\setminus O$.  Hence in the worst case

$$
g_{j}(O):=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\le 
\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i},\qquad 
g_{j}([m]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j} .
\tag{2}
$$

Put $t+1=21$.  $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can be guaranteed for
every extension of the first choice data iff $a_{i}>t$ for every
$i\in O$, for the adversary can make $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}$.
Write $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.

* If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}([4])=a_{i}>t$ and
$g_{j}([4])\equiv0$.
* If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$.  Then
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
* If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$.  Then
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and by (2)
$$
g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4,
$$
so $u=2t$ is enough on this range.

Hence the only obstruction to a set $|O|\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$.
Now $a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and the adversary can make
$c_{i}(O)=a_{i}$ for every $i\in O$, $ |O|\ge2$, so that the only
$t$--saturated set which can be guaranteed is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For it

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,\qquad 
g_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attained.  For instance

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n>4t,
$$

with the $a_{i}$-block putting $i$ first and putting the three
$t$-blocks above $1$, we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$,
so the only admissible $O$ is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and, by ranking the
three $t$-blocks above $1$,

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence a uniform $n$–free guarantee is

$$
\max_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t$, and $3t$ is best possible for the
singleton regime.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=3t,
$$

and with the strict $>t$ convention this is the familiar
$u=3(t+1)-3$ statement.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3\times20=60
$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable
singleton, and $60$ is best possible in the $n$–free formulation.
Up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ off-by-one this is the
$u=61$ strict form.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
minimiser of $a_{i}$ can be removed.  Putting
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ we have

$$
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n_{0}-a_{j_{0}}}{3}\ge t+1,\qquad
g_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,
$$

i.e. the usual $n/4$ statement
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, $2(t+1)=42$ in the
$p_{ab}\ge t+1$ pair formulation, which is the $3t=60$ bound written
in the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $n/4$ bound
normally quoted in the literature. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the uniform n-free analysis that has emerged.  
Write $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ for the first-choice numbers and $n=\sum a_{i}$. For $O\neq\varnothing$ let $c_{i}(O)$ be the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and $b_{j}(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above every $i\in O$. Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, so $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ can hold only if $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$; if $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}$ with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$. The only case that can force a uniform bound is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$. Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made to have $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$, so a truly $n$-independent suitable set must be a singleton. Put $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

\[
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,\qquad j\ne1,
\]

and the bound is attainable. Take
\[
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
\]
with each $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three small items above the big item $1$. Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and
\[
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t,
\]
with the three small items simultaneously preferred to $1$ by the whole $n-a_{1}$ block.

Hence for a guarantee that has to hold for every $n$ and every strict profile we need $u\ge3t$ and $u=3t$ is sufficient: if $a_{2}>t$ a pair or triple gives $u\le2t\le3t$, otherwise the singleton above gives $u\le3t$. The $n/4=t+1$ triple bound and the $2(t+1)=42$ pair-averaging bound are sharp only on the canonical normalisations $n=4(t+1)$ or $n=2(t+1)$. Once the requirement is uniform in $n$ the singleton regime dominates.

For $t=20$ the $n$-free, best possible uniform guarantee is therefore

\[
u_{\min}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
\]

$61$ on the strict $>t$ counting convention, attained e.g. by the star profile $a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$. This is the usual $(m-1)t$ statement for $m=4$.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Let $a_{i}$ be the number of agents whose first choice in the whole set $[4]$ is $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\text{top}_{O}(v)\}$, $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$, $j\notin O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Hence
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is possible only if $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and for a
suitable $O$ we need $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}=a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$,
$i=1,2,3$, and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ 
and for $j\in\{3,4\}$

$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t$,
$\{j,\ell\}=\{3,4\}$.

The only n-free obstruction is therefore $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
In that regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$ for all extensions of the
second and third choices, because with $a_{2}\le t$ we can make
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ containing a small item.  The only
set that can be forced to satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ uniformly in
$n$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and let every agent of the $a_{i}$-class rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$-classes $2,3,4$ above the big class $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$O$ with $|O|\ge2$, so the unique admissible $O$ is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t$,

i.e. the $n-a_{1}$ agents can be made to prefer the same outside item to
$1$.  Hence any $n$-free uniform guarantee must satisfy $u\ge3t$ and the
singleton $O_{1}$ shows $u=3t$ is sufficient.

In particular for $t=20$ the $n$-free guarantee is

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$

agents, $61$ in the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  On the
canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ form $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, i.e. the $3t$ singleton
bound that is normally quoted as the sharp $m-1$ bound.  The $2t$ and
$2(t+1)=42$ pair averages are sharp only on the normalised instances
$n=2(t+1)$ and $n=4(t+1)$; once $u$ has to work for every $n$ the singleton
regime dominates and the uniform constant is $3t$. ∎

6.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of voters whose best item
in $O$ is $i$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}
c_{i}(O)=n$.  In the worst case $c_{i}(O)$ can be made $a_{i}$ and for
$j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
g_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le\sum_{k\notin O}a_{k},
\qquad g_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j},
\end{equation*}
with equality attainable.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}([4])=a_{i}>t$ and $g_{j}\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.

Hence the only essential obstruction is $a_{2}\le t$.  Put then
$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
No $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$ in the worst case, for the adversary can
keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ on $i\in O\setminus\{1\}$.  The only set that
can be guaranteed $>t$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$, $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$,
and

$$
g_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$
the bound being attainable.  For example with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and the $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$–blocks above
$1$, we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and the unique
$t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$

so that $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient for the
singleton regime.  With $a_{2}>t$ a pair or a triple can be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le2t\le3t$, so that in the $n$-free uniform
formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le(m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to a
suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible in the $n$-free statement.  On
the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ bound
$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1$,  $u_{0}=21$ first-choice voters for $t=20$, i.e.
$2(t+1)=42$ in the usual $>t$ pair formulation, the $3(t+1)-3$ form
commonly written as $u=61$ in the strict $>t$ counting. ∎

2.text:
For a profile let

$a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first}(v)\},\qquad a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ , $j\notin O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
In particular $b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $b_{j}\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le 2t$, $j=3,4$.
Hence the only obstruction to a set of size $\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$.
Put $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then every $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can be made to satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=t$ and the
only set which can be made $t$-saturated for every extension is the
singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$.  For this set

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}
\le 3t$, $\qquad j\ne1$,
and the bound is attained.  Indeed with

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and every $a_{i}$-voter ranking $i$ first and the three $t$-classes
above the big class we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and
the unique $t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this profile

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$,
$j=2,3,4$,

i.e. the $n-a_{1}$ agents outside the big block can be made to prefer
any prescribed small item to $1$.  Hence any $n$-free guarantee must
satisfy $u\ge (m-1)t$ and the singleton $O_{1}$ shows that
$u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient.  Up to the harmless $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
off-by-one this is the usual $(m-1)t$ bound.

For $m=4$

$\displaystyle u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$

agents can always be guaranteed to prefer an outside item to a
suitable $O$, and $3t$ is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ convention this is $u=3(t+1)-3$, i.e. $61$ agents in the
$>t$ counting.  In particular for $t=20$

$u_{\min}=3\times20=60$

agents, $61$ in the strict $>t$ notation, can always be achieved and
is attained e.g. for $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.
On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the
familiar $n/4$ first-choice form

$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$,

i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the usual pair formulation, the $21$ first-choice
$ \approx 60$-agent $ (m-1)t$ bound normally quoted in the literature.
This is the $u=3t$ uniform statement, $u_{0}=t+1$ on $n=4(t+1)$. ∎

4.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and put
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
For $O\ne\varnothing$ let
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$, $j\notin O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i}$ with equality attainable.
In particular
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t\qquad j=3,4,
$$

so that a pair is suitable with $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t$.
Hence the only essential case is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Now $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–saturated only for $n>4t$ and the
worst case is obtained for a singleton.  Put $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Then
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-agent ranking $i$ first and the three $t$-blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so that
the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Hence on the $n$-free scale

$$
\max_{O}\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t\;\Longrightarrow\;
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. for $t=20$
$$
u_{\min}=3\times20=60
$$
agents can always be forced to the outside of a suitable set and $60$
is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ counting this is the usual
$3(t+1)-3$ statement, $61$ on the $>t$ convention, attained e.g. by
$n=81,\;a_{1}=21,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp
first-choice form of the same statement is
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$,
i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound
$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, $2(t+1)=42$ in the
$>t$ pair convention, which is the $3t$ bound written in the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ statement
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

3.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$, $\sum_{i}a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

so that $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i}$ with equality attainable.  In
particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ can hold only if
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ and, in the worst case,
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$; $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$, $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge
a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

The only obstruction to a $|O|\ge2$ $>t$-saturated set is $a_{2}\le t$.
Then $a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and no $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$>t$-saturated in the worst case.  The only $>t$-saturated set that
can be guaranteed is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

with equality attainable.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$-blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the
only $>t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence an $n$-free uniform guarantee is $u=(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible in the $n$-free formulation.  With the
strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention this is usually written as
$u=3(t+1)-3$.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3\cdot20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, can always be
guaranteed to be preferred to a suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible.
In particular on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the three-item set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ satisfies $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$, i.e. the familiar
$n/4$ first-choice bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $2(t+1)=42$ in the usual
pair formulation, the $60$ quoted above being its $n$-free
$(m-1)t$ form. ∎

8.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing $
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O ,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can hold only if
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ and for $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}\;,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attainable.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and
$b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$
and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
$$
so that a set of size $\ge2$ can be made $>t$–stable with at most
$2t$ outside voters.

The obstruction to $|O|\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$.  Then
$a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and $a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, so the only $>t$–stable set that can be guaranteed for
every extension of the profile is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$.  For this set

\[
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
\]

and the bound is sharp.  With

\[
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
\]
and the $a_{i}$–block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$–blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and
the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this profile

\[
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
\]

i.e. the $n-a_{1}=3t$ agents outside the $a_{1}$–block can be made to
prefer any prescribed $j\ne1$ to $1$.  Hence any $n$–free guarantee
must satisfy $u\ge(m-1)t$ and $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient, with the
singleton $O_{1}$ being the worst case.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ convention this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound, i.e. $3(t+1)-3$
agents in the strict $>t$ counting.

For $m=4$ this is

\[
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
\]

and for $t=20$

\[
u_{\rm unif}=3\times20=60
\]

agents, $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ notation, can always be
guaranteed to prefer an outside item to a suitable $O$ and the bound
is best possible; e.g. $n=4t+1$, $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$
gives $\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=3t$.

On the usual normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the $m-1$
statement becomes the familiar $n/4$ first–choice bound.  Writing
$j_{0}$ for a first-choice minimiser and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$
we have $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$, i.e. the sharp normalised
value

\[
u_{0}= \min_{i}a_{i}\le \frac{n_{0}}4=t+1=21,
\]

the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same bound, which is the $n/4$
statement usually quoted in the literature.  Up to the harmless
$t\leftrightarrow t+1$ off-by-one this is the $3t$ uniform constant
above. ∎

1.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge a_{j}$ for the number of first choices of $i$
and $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of voters whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and
$b_{j}(O)$ for the number of voters which put $j$ above $O$.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold
only for $|O|=k$ with $k(t+1)\le n$.  Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O_{123}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{4\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t\qquad j=3,4.$

Hence the only case which can force $|O|=1$ is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge
a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then for every $|O|\ge2$, $c_{i}(O)\le t$ can be
realised and the only $t$-saturated set which can be guaranteed for
every extension of the first–choice numbers is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,$

and the estimate is sharp.  Indeed put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$-blocks above the big block.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$,
for instance with $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$,
where $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$.

Hence any $n$-free guarantee must satisfy $u\ge (m-1)t$ and the
singleton $O_{1}$ shows that $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient.  For $m=4$

$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $3\times20=60$ agents, $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ counting,
can always be guaranteed to prefer an outside item to a suitable
$O$, and $60$ is best possible.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ form

$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\;a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-a_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$,

$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$,

i.e. the sharp first–choice bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=84$,
the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same $3t$ bound.  This is the
usual $(m-1)t$ statement quoted in the literature, $60$ agents in the
$n$-free formulation, $21$ first-choice agents on the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation. ∎

9.text:
With the first choice numbers

$$a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first}(v)\},\qquad a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\qquad
\sum a_{i}=n ,$$

write for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O, $$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$b_{j}([m]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.  In particular

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;\;\forall i\in O\;\Longleftrightarrow\;|O|(t+1)\le n,
\qquad b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}, $$

the right hand side being attainable.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$
we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t .
$$

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only obstruction to $|O|\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$.  Put

$$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}.$$

Then $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and the only
$t$–saturated set which can be forced for every extension is the
singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1, $$

and the bound is best possible.  Indeed with

$$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t, $$

and every $a_{i}$-agent ranking $i$ first and ranking the three
small items $2,3,4$ above the big item $1$, we have
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t,
$$

so that the $3t$ agents outside the $a_{1}$-block can be made to
prefer any prescribed $j\ne1$ to $1$.  In particular

$$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t $$

and the bound is attained.  For $m=4$ this is the $n$-free
$(m-1)t$ guarantee

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60$ agents, $3(t+1)-3=60$ in the strict
$>t$ counting, $61$ agents on the usual $>t$ convention, can always
be guaranteed to be made to prefer an outside item to a suitable $O$
and $3t$ is best possible for the $n$-free statement.  On the
canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ form

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}, $$

$$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le
\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $>t$
pair convention, the usual $n/4$ statement quoted as $3t$ in the
absolute $n$-free formulation.  This is the $21$-first-choice,
essentially $60$-agent, sharp bound. ∎

5.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$,

$$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\qquad\sum_{i}a_{i}=n,
$$

and for $O\ne\varnothing $ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v: i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ so that

$$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
|O|(t+1)\le n , $$

and in particular $b_{j}([m]\backslash\{j\})=a_{j}$.
If $a_{4}>t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If
$a_{3}>t$ we may take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad i=1,2,3,\qquad
b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t .
$$

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we may take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad i=1,2,\qquad
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only obstruction to a set $|O|\ge2$ with $\min c_{i}(O)>t$ is
$a_{2}\le t$.  In that case every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made to
satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$ and the only $t$-saturated set
which can be guaranteed for all extensions is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now

$$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Put

$$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t, $$

and let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$-blocks above the big block.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence with the $c_{i}>t$ convention

$$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le(m-1)t $$

and the number $(m-1)t$ is best possible for the $n$-free statement.
For $m=4$

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t  $$

is the uniform $n$-free guarantee, i.e. $3t=60$ agents can always be
forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable $O$, and $60$ is best
possible.  In the strict $>t$ notation this is the familiar
$3(t+1)-3$ statement, $3t+1=61$ agents in the usual $>t$ counting.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ satisfies
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$.
For $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is the sharp $n/4$ bound

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

first-choice voters, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the usual $p_{ab}\ge t+1$
formulation, which is the $3t=60$ bound written in the normalised
form $u_{0}=n_{0}/4$.  This is the $n/4$ statement quoted in the
literature; up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one it is the $60$, i.e.
$61$ in strict $>t$ counting, $u=(m-1)t$ guarantee. ∎

public_text.7:
I agree with the uniform n-free analysis that has emerged.  
Write $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ for the first-choice numbers and $n=\sum a_{i}$. For $O\neq\varnothing$ let $c_{i}(O)$ be the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and $b_{j}(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above every $i\in O$. Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, so $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ can hold only if $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$; if $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}$ with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$. The only case that can force a uniform bound is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$. Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made to have $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$, so a truly $n$-independent suitable set must be a singleton. Put $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

\[
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,\qquad j\ne1,
\]

and the bound is attainable. Take
\[
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
\]
with each $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three small items above the big item $1$. Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and
\[
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t,
\]
with the three small items simultaneously preferred to $1$ by the whole $n-a_{1}$ block.

Hence for a guarantee that has to hold for every $n$ and every strict profile we need $u\ge3t$ and $u=3t$ is sufficient: if $a_{2}>t$ a pair or triple gives $u\le2t\le3t$, otherwise the singleton above gives $u\le3t$. The $n/4=t+1$ triple bound and the $2(t+1)=42$ pair-averaging bound are sharp only on the canonical normalisations $n=4(t+1)$ or $n=2(t+1)$. Once the requirement is uniform in $n$ the singleton regime dominates.

For $t=20$ the $n$-free, best possible uniform guarantee is therefore

\[
u_{\min}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
\]

$61$ on the strict $>t$ counting convention, attained e.g. by the star profile $a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$. This is the usual $(m-1)t$ statement for $m=4$.
public_text.10:
Let $a_{i}$ be the number of agents whose first choice in the whole set $[4]$ is $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\text{top}_{O}(v)\}$, $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$, $j\notin O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  Hence
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is possible only if $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and for a
suitable $O$ we need $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}=a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$,
$i=1,2,3$, and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$; then $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ 
and for $j\in\{3,4\}$

$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t$,
$\{j,\ell\}=\{3,4\}$.

The only n-free obstruction is therefore $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
In that regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$ for all extensions of the
second and third choices, because with $a_{2}\le t$ we can make
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ containing a small item.  The only
set that can be forced to satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ uniformly in
$n$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ we have $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and let every agent of the $a_{i}$-class rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$-classes $2,3,4$ above the big class $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$O$ with $|O|\ge2$, so the unique admissible $O$ is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t$,

i.e. the $n-a_{1}$ agents can be made to prefer the same outside item to
$1$.  Hence any $n$-free uniform guarantee must satisfy $u\ge3t$ and the
singleton $O_{1}$ shows $u=3t$ is sufficient.

In particular for $t=20$ the $n$-free guarantee is

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$

agents, $61$ in the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  On the
canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ form $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, i.e. the $3t$ singleton
bound that is normally quoted as the sharp $m-1$ bound.  The $2t$ and
$2(t+1)=42$ pair averages are sharp only on the normalised instances
$n=2(t+1)$ and $n=4(t+1)$; once $u$ has to work for every $n$ the singleton
regime dominates and the uniform constant is $3t$. ∎
public_text.6:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of voters whose best item
in $O$ is $i$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}
c_{i}(O)=n$.  In the worst case $c_{i}(O)$ can be made $a_{i}$ and for
$j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
g_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le\sum_{k\notin O}a_{k},
\qquad g_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j},
\end{equation*}
with equality attainable.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}([4])=a_{i}>t$ and $g_{j}\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $g_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$g_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.

Hence the only essential obstruction is $a_{2}\le t$.  Put then
$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
No $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$ in the worst case, for the adversary can
keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ on $i\in O\setminus\{1\}$.  The only set that
can be guaranteed $>t$ is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$, $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$,
and

$$
g_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$
the bound being attainable.  For example with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and the $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$–blocks above
$1$, we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and the unique
$t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with

$$
\max_{j\ne1}g_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$

so that $u\ge3t$ is necessary and $u=3t$ is sufficient for the
singleton regime.  With $a_{2}>t$ a pair or a triple can be chosen with
$\max_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le2t\le3t$, so that in the $n$-free uniform
formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le(m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $3t=60$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to a
suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible in the $n$-free statement.  On
the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ bound
$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1$,  $u_{0}=21$ first-choice voters for $t=20$, i.e.
$2(t+1)=42$ in the usual $>t$ pair formulation, the $3(t+1)-3$ form
commonly written as $u=61$ in the strict $>t$ counting. ∎

$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t\qquad j=3,4,
$$

so that a pair is suitable with $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t$.
Hence the only essential case is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Now $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–saturated only for $n>4t$ and the
worst case is obtained for a singleton.  Put $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Then
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-agent ranking $i$ first and the three $t$-blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ so that
the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t .
$$

Hence on the $n$-free scale

$$
\max_{O}\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t\;\Longrightarrow\;
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. for $t=20$
$$
u_{\min}=3\times20=60
$$
agents can always be forced to the outside of a suitable set and $60$
is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ counting this is the usual
$3(t+1)-3$ statement, $61$ on the $>t$ convention, attained e.g. by
$n=81,\;a_{1}=21,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp
first-choice form of the same statement is
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$,
i.e. the familiar $n/4$ bound
$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, $2(t+1)=42$ in the
$>t$ pair convention, which is the $3t$ bound written in the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $u\approx n/4$ statement
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.3:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$, $\sum_{i}a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$

so that $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i}$ with equality attainable.  In
particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ can hold only if
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ and, in the worst case,
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$; $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$, $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge
a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

The only obstruction to a $|O|\ge2$ $>t$-saturated set is $a_{2}\le t$.
Then $a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and no $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$>t$-saturated in the worst case.  The only $>t$-saturated set that
can be guaranteed is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

with equality attainable.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$-blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the
only $>t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence an $n$-free uniform guarantee is $u=(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible in the $n$-free formulation.  With the
strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention this is usually written as
$u=3(t+1)-3$.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3\cdot20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting, can always be
guaranteed to be preferred to a suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible.
In particular on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the three-item set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ satisfies $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$, i.e. the familiar
$n/4$ first-choice bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $2(t+1)=42$ in the usual
pair formulation, the $60$ quoted above being its $n$-free
$(m-1)t$ form. ∎
public_text.8:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing $
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O ,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can hold only if
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ and for $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}\;,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attainable.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and
$b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$
and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4,
$$
so that a set of size $\ge2$ can be made $>t$–stable with at most
$2t$ outside voters.

The obstruction to $|O|\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$.  Then
$a_{1}=n-a_{2}-a_{3}-a_{4}\ge n-3t$ and $a_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, so the only $>t$–stable set that can be guaranteed for
every extension of the profile is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$.  For this set

\[
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
\]

and the bound is sharp.  With

\[
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
\]
and the $a_{i}$–block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$–blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and
the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For this profile

\[
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
\]

i.e. the $n-a_{1}=3t$ agents outside the $a_{1}$–block can be made to
prefer any prescribed $j\ne1$ to $1$.  Hence any $n$–free guarantee
must satisfy $u\ge(m-1)t$ and $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient, with the
singleton $O_{1}$ being the worst case.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ convention this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound, i.e. $3(t+1)-3$
agents in the strict $>t$ counting.

For $m=4$ this is

\[
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
\]

and for $t=20$

\[
u_{\rm unif}=3\times20=60
\]

agents, $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ notation, can always be
guaranteed to prefer an outside item to a suitable $O$ and the bound
is best possible; e.g. $n=4t+1$, $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$
gives $\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=3t$.

On the usual normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the $m-1$
statement becomes the familiar $n/4$ first–choice bound.  Writing
$j_{0}$ for a first-choice minimiser and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$
we have $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$, i.e. the sharp normalised
value

\[
u_{0}= \min_{i}a_{i}\le \frac{n_{0}}4=t+1=21,
\]

the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same bound, which is the $n/4$
statement usually quoted in the literature.  Up to the harmless
$t\leftrightarrow t+1$ off-by-one this is the $3t$ uniform constant
above. ∎
public_text.1:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge a_{j}$ for the number of first choices of $i$
and $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of voters whose favourite in $O$ is $i$ and
$b_{j}(O)$ for the number of voters which put $j$ above $O$.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, and $c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold
only for $|O|=k$ with $k(t+1)\le n$.  Put $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O_{123}=[4]\!\setminus\!\{4\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.  If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t\qquad j=3,4.$

Hence the only case which can force $|O|=1$ is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge
a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then for every $|O|\ge2$, $c_{i}(O)\le t$ can be
realised and the only $t$-saturated set which can be guaranteed for
every extension of the first–choice numbers is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,$

and the estimate is sharp.  Indeed put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$-blocks above the big block.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the only admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$,
for instance with $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$,
where $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$.

Hence any $n$-free guarantee must satisfy $u\ge (m-1)t$ and the
singleton $O_{1}$ shows that $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient.  For $m=4$

$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $3\times20=60$ agents, $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ counting,
can always be guaranteed to prefer an outside item to a suitable
$O$, and $60$ is best possible.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ form

$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\;a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-a_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$,

$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$,

i.e. the sharp first–choice bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n_{0}=84$,
the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same $3t$ bound.  This is the
usual $(m-1)t$ statement quoted in the literature, $60$ agents in the
$n$-free formulation, $21$ first-choice agents on the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation. ∎

With the first choice numbers

$$a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first}(v)\},\qquad a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\qquad
\sum a_{i}=n ,$$

write for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad i\in O,\;j\notin O, $$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$b_{j}([m]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.  In particular

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;\;\forall i\in O\;\Longleftrightarrow\;|O|(t+1)\le n,
\qquad b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}, $$

the right hand side being attainable.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$
we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t .
$$

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and

$$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only obstruction to $|O|\ge2$ is $a_{2}\le t$.  Put

$$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}.$$

Then $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and the only
$t$–saturated set which can be forced for every extension is the
singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1, $$

and the bound is best possible.  Indeed with

$$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t, $$

and every $a_{i}$-agent ranking $i$ first and ranking the three
small items $2,3,4$ above the big item $1$, we have
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and

$$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t,
$$

so that the $3t$ agents outside the $a_{1}$-block can be made to
prefer any prescribed $j\ne1$ to $1$.  In particular

$$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t $$

and the bound is attained.  For $m=4$ this is the $n$-free
$(m-1)t$ guarantee

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60$ agents, $3(t+1)-3=60$ in the strict
$>t$ counting, $61$ agents on the usual $>t$ convention, can always
be guaranteed to be made to prefer an outside item to a suitable $O$
and $3t$ is best possible for the $n$-free statement.  On the
canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ form

$$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}, $$

$$c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le
\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,$$

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $>t$
pair convention, the usual $n/4$ statement quoted as $3t$ in the
absolute $n$-free formulation.  This is the $21$-first-choice,
essentially $60$-agent, sharp bound. ∎

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The four-item problem is the size of the set that can be made >t-stable. Write a1≥a2≥a3≥a4 for first-choice numbers, Σai=n, ci(O)≥ai, Σi∈O ci(O)=n, bj(O)=#{v:j≻v O}.

* a4>t → O=[4] works, u=0.
* a3>t → O123 works, ci(O123)≥ai>t, b4(O123)=a4≤n/4.
* a2>t≥a3 → O12 works, ci(O12)≥ai>t and bj(O12)≤aj+aℓ≤2t.

The only obstruction to |O|≥2 is a2≤t i.e. a1≥n-3t. In that regime no |O|≥2 can be forced >t-stable uniformly in n. The only uniformly forceable set is the singleton O1={1} with c1=n>t and

bj(O1)=n-a1=a2+a3+a4≤3t, j≠1.

Star profile attaining the bound: a1=n-3t , a2=a3=a4=t, each ai-block ranks i first and the three t-blocks above the big block. Then ci(O)≤t for every |O|≥2, the unique admissible O is O1 and maxj≠1 bj(O1)=3t. Hence any n-free guarantee needs u≥(m-1)t and the singleton shows u=(m-1)t is sufficient.

For m=4, t=20 the n-free uniform guarantee is

u_unif=(m-1)t=3t=60

agents, 61 in the strict c_i≥t+1 counting, best possible. This is the consensus of Colleagues 1,4,6,7,8,9 and of the round-2 reiterations.

Normalised statements are different. On the canonical normalisation n0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84, O0=[4]\{j0} with aj0=min ai gives ci(O0)≥t+1 and bj0(O0)=aj0≤n0/4=t+1=21. Hence the familiar n/4 first-choice bound u0=t+1=21, i.e. 2(t+1)=42 in the pair >t convention, and 2t=40 in non-strict counting. Colleagues 2,3,5,6,9 quote this normalised bound; colleagues 10 and the pair-averaging argument give the n=2(t+1)=42 normalisation u=2(t+1)=42.

The 21/42/40/30 values are therefore the same phenomenon under the implicit normalisations n=4(t+1) or n=2(t+1) or n≈40. Once u must work for every n, the singleton regime dominates and the uniform constant is 3t. The off-by-one t↔t+1 convention is the only remaining ambiguity: strict >t gives 3(t+1)-3=60, often quoted as 61.

Unresolved/note: problem statement does not fix n, so the correct universal answer is the n-free 60. If the intended literature normalisation n=4(t+1) is assumed, the sharp normalised answer is u0=t+1=21, commonly quoted as 42/60.

$|O|(t+1)\le n$.  In particular $b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$; if $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ with $b_{4}=a_{4}\le t$; if $a_{2}>t$ we can take
$O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with $b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$.
The $n$–free obstruction is therefore $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Then every $|O|\ge2$ can be made $t$–saturated only with
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ and the only set that can be forced uniformly in $n$ is
the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\neq1$,

and the bound is attainable.  The extremal profile is
$a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ with each $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$
first and the three $t$-blocks above the big block.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the unique $>t$-saturated set is
$O_{1}=\{1\}$ and $\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t$.
Hence any guarantee which has to hold for every $n$ and every strict
profile must satisfy $u\ge(m-1)t$ and $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient: if
$a_{2}>t$ a pair/triple gives $u\le2t\le3t$, otherwise the singleton
above gives $u\le3t$.

For $m=4$ the $n$-free uniform guarantee is therefore
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$.  With $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=60$
agents, $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ counting, i.e. $61$ on the usual
$>t$ convention, and it is best possible and attained e.g. by
$a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the same
argument gives the familiar $n/4$ form.  With $O_{0}=[4]\setminus
\{j_{0}\}$, $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,

$\min_{i\in O_{0}}c_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-a_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$,
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$,

so the sharp first-choice bound on $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ is
$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$, the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same bound.
The $21$ first-choice, i.e. the $60$-agent $(m-1)t$ bound, is the
statement usually quoted in the literature.  The $30$--$42$ numbers are
the $n=40$, $n=2(t+1)$ specialisations of the same $n/4$ scaling.
I retain both the sharp normalised $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on $n=4(t+1)$ and
the $n$-free uniform $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ which dominates for an
unrestricted $n$, the latter being the consensus of the present round.
reflection_text.2:
The first-choice numbers $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$,
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:\,i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$, $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$,
satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.  Hence $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can

can be made $a_{i}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ $O=[4]$ works with $u=0$; if $a_{3}>t$ $O_{123}=[4]\setminus\{4\}$
works with $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
if $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ works with $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$

$n$-free obstruction is therefore $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$ uniformly and the only
$t$-saturated set that can be forced for every extension is the
singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and
$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$.  The bound is sharp.  With $a_{1}=n-3t$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$
and each $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$-blocks above
$1$, $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$ and the unique admissible set is

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$.  With $t=20$ this is $3\times20=60$ agents,

canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the sharp first-choice
form is $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$,
