reflection_text.3:
The first-choice numbers dominate. Write $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, $c_{i}(O)$ the number of voters whose top in $O$ is $i$
and $b_{j}(O)$ the number of voters who put $j$ above the whole of $O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{i\notin O}a_{i}$ with equality attainable.

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  Hence

* $a_{4}>t\;\Rightarrow\;O=[4]$, $b_{j}\equiv0$;
* $a_{3}>t\;\Rightarrow\;O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ works, $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$
and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
* $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}\;\Rightarrow\;O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ works,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$,
$j=3,4$.

The only n-free obstruction is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$ uniformly and the only set that can
be guaranteed $>t$ for every extension of the second and third choices
is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now

$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$,

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,

and the bound is tight.  Put
$a_{1}=n-3t,\ a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$
first and rank the three $t$-blocks above the big block. Then
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is
$O_{1}=\{1\}$ and $\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=3t$.
Hence any guarantee which has to hold for every $n$ and every profile
needs $u\ge(m-1)t$ and $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient.

For $m=4$

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$,

best possible in the $n$-free formulation.  With the strict $>t$
convention this is the usual $3(t+1)-3$ statement.  For $t=20$

$u_{\rm univ}=3\times20=60$,

$61$ on the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}\ge t+1$.  The extremal star
profile is $a_{1}=n-60,\ a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, e.g. $n=81$,
$a_{1}=21,\ a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, with
$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=60$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the same
construction becomes the familiar $n/4$ first-choice bound.
With $j_{0}$ a first-choice minimiser $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ we
have $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4$,
i.e. the sharp normalised value

$u_{0}=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$,

the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form that is usually quoted.  This is the
$21$ first-choice, $60$-agent $(m-1)t$ bound normally quoted in the
literature; the $2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ pair averages are sharp only on the
normalised instances $n=2(t+1)$ and $n=4(t+1)$.  Once $u$ is required
to be independent of $n$ the singleton regime dominates and the
uniform constant is $3t=60$, $21$ first-choice voters on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $u=3t$ statement is the one all
colleagues in round 2 converge to; the $u=t+1=21$, $u=2(t+1)=42$ figures
are the same bound written in the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’ll put the uniform-in-n counting on the table in the first-choice notation that everyone is using.

Let $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ be the first-choice numbers, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\neq\varnothing$
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\ \forall i\in O\}$, $j\notin O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$, with $b_{j}(O)\le\sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}$ attainable.

If $a_{4}>t$ take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$; $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t$ take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$; $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.

Hence the only $n$-free obstruction is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
In that regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be forced to satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$
for every extension of the second and third choices, because the adversary
can keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ on $i\in O\setminus\{1\}$. The only set that
can be guaranteed $>t$-saturated uniformly in $n$ is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and
$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$
and the bound is sharp. Put
$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$
and let each $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three $t$-blocks
$2,3,4$ above the big block $1$. Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$,
the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and
$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$
e.g. $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ gives $\max b_{j}=60$.

Thus any $n$-free guarantee must satisfy $u\ge(m-1)t$ and the singleton
$O_{1}$ shows $u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient; with $a_{2}>t$ a pair or triple
gives $\max b_{j}\le2t\le3t$. For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

and in the strict $c_{i}>t$ convention this is $3(t+1)-3$, i.e. $61$
agents in the $>t$ counting. For $t=20$ this is the uniform best possible
$u=3\times20=60$. The familiar $n/4=t+1=21$ first-choice bound and the
$2(t+1)=42$ pair average are sharp only on the normalisations
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ resp. $n=2(t+1)$; once $u$ has to work for every $n$
the singleton regime dominates and the uniform constant is $3t$. ∎

3.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$,
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le \sum_{k\notin O}a_{k}$ with equality attainable.
In particular $c_{i}(O)>t$ for every $i\in O$ can hold only for
$|O|(t+1)\le n$ and $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and
$b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only $n$–free obstruction is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

for then $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–saturated only for $n>4t$ and in
the worst case the only set which can be forced to satisfy
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ for every extension of the second and third
choices is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For $O_{1}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the estimate is sharp.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$–block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$–blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the
unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

For instance $n=4t+1$, $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ gives
$c_{1}(O_{1})=t+1>t$ and $b_{j}(O_{1})=3t$ for $j=2,3,4$.  Hence

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible for an $n$–free guarantee.  With
$a_{2}>t$ a pair or a triple can be chosen with $\max_{j\notin O}
b_{j}(O)\le2t\le3t$, so the singleton $O_{1}$ is the worst case.

For $m=4$ this is the uniform $n$–free bound

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=3\times20=60$ agents can always be forced to lie
outside a suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible.  In the usual
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict notation this is the familiar $3(t+1)-3$
statement, $61$ agents in the $>t$ counting, attained e.g. by the
star profile $a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$,
for which the only $>t$–saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and
$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=60$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ first-choice form $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$, i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$
pair form of the same $3t$ bound.  This is the $60$, essentially
$21$ first-choice, $(m-1)t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

6.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and put
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, 
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$, $j\notin O$.
Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$; if $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$; if $a_{2}>t\ge
a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and
$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.
Hence the only $n$–free obstruction is
$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
In that case
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ can be forced for every $|O|\ge2$ and the only
$t$-saturated set which can be guaranteed for every extension of the
profile is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

For $O_{1}$ $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,

and the bound is attainable.  Put $a_{1}=n-3t$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$
and let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three $t$
blocks above the big block $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$,

e.g. $n=81,\;a_{1}=21,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$
for $j=2,3,4$.  Hence any $n$-free guarantee needs $u\ge(m-1)t$ and
$u=(m-1)t$ is sufficient, the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$ being the worst
case.  With the usual $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention this is the
$3(t+1)-3$ statement.

For $m=4$ the uniform constant is
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$.
In particular for $t=20$

$u_{\min}=3\times20=60$

agents can always be forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable
$O$, and $60$ is best possible in the $n$-free formulation, $3(t+1)-3$
$=$ $61$ on the strict $>t$ counting.  On the canonical
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ form
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of
the same $(m-1)t$ bound. ∎

8.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$,
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\;\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.  In particular $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$
is possible only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$; if $a_{3}>t$
$O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ gives $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$; if $a_{2}>t$ 
$O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ gives $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{j}+a_{\ell}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence a set $|O|\ge2$ with $\min c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced uniformly
in $n$ only while $a_{2}>t$.  The $n$--free obstruction is
$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can then be made
$>t$–saturated in the worst case and the only set which can be
guaranteed for every extension of the first choices is the singleton

$$
O_{1}=\{1\},\qquad c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,
$$

for which

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Put $a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$
and let every $a_{i}$–block rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$–blocks above the big block $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is $O_{1}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence for an $n$–free guarantee

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced to the outside of a suitable $O$ and $3t$
is sharp.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $3(t+1)-3$ and $61$ on the usual strict $>t$ counting,
can always be guaranteed and is attained e.g. by
$a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ form
$u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, $2(t+1)=42$ in the pair form,
the $3t$ bound written in the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

2.text:
For a profile write

$$
a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first}(v)\},\qquad a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
\qquad\sum a_{i}=n ,
$$

and for $\emptyset\ne O\subset[m]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and in the worst
case $c_{i}(O)$ can be made $a_{i}$.  In particular
$b_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$ and

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  
If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ with $b_{j}\equiv0$;
if $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
if $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only $n$-free obstruction to a set with $|O|\ge2$ is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

and then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-saturated uniformly in the
second and third choices.  The only set which can be guaranteed for
every extension is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For it

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1 .
$$

The bound is best possible.  With

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three
$t$-blocks above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$ and the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence in the $n$-free formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced to the outside of a $>t$-saturated set and
$3t$ is best possible.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, $61$ in the strict $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, can always be
realised and is attained e.g. by $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$,
with $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$.  Up to the harmless $t\leftrightarrow
t+1$ off-by-one this is the usual $(m-1)t$ statement.

Remark.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
sharp first-choice form is $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$, $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$.  Hence the normally quoted
$n/4$ bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$
pair form of the same $3t$ bound, the $60$ above being its $n$-free
$(m-1)t$ expression.  This is the $u=3(t+1)-3=61$ strict $>t$ form
commonly written in the literature. ∎

5.text:
For the first choice numbers write

$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},\;\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\emptyset$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O $.

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.  In particular

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and
$c_{i}(O)>t$ can be guaranteed in the worst case only by
$a_{i}>t$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, if $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$ and if
$a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4.$

Hence the $n$–free obstruction is

$a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},$

for then no $|O|\ge 2$ can be made $>t$-saturated in the worst
extension of the second and third choices.  The only set which can be
forced to satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ uniformly in $n$ is the
singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now

$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t\qquad {\rm and}\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t,
\;j\ne1,$

and the bound is attainable.  Put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

and let every $a_{i}$–block rank $i$ first and rank the three
$t$-blocks $2,3,4$ above the big block $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for
every $|O|\ge2$, the unique $>t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$

e.g. $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$ for
$j=2,3,4$.  Hence any $n$-free uniform guarantee must satisfy
$u\ge(m-1)t$ and the singleton $O_{1}$ shows that $u=(m-1)t$ is
sufficient, the worst case being the star profile above.

In particular for $m=4$

$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t$

agents can always be forced to the outside of a suitable $O$ and $3t$
is best possible in the $n$–free formulation.  For $t=20$ this is

$u_{\min}=3\times20=60$

agents, i.e. $b_{j}(O_{1})\le60$ for the essentially unique suitable
set $O_{1}=\{1\}$, and the bound is attained by the star profile
$a_{1}=n-60$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$.  On the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$, $b_{j}(O)\le u$ convention this is the familiar
$3(t+1)-3$ i.e. $61$ agents in the usual $>t$ off–by–one notation,
the $n/4=t+1=21$ first–choice, $2(t+1)=42$ pair form on the
canonical normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$.  This is the customary
$(m-1)t$ $n/4$ bound. ∎

9.text:
With $a_{i}$ the first choice numbers $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  In particular
$b_{j}\bigl([4]\setminus\{j\}\bigr)=a_{j}$ and $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$
can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  If $a_{4}>t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and
$b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we may take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and

$$
c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad i=1,2,3,\qquad 
b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t .
$$

If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we may take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and

$$
c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence a set $|O|\ge2$ with $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced
iff $a_{2}>t$.  The $n$–free obstruction is therefore

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4} .
$$

In that regime every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made to satisfy
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$ and the only set which can be made
$t$-saturated for every extension of the second and third choices is
the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For $O_{1}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  With

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n>4t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three
$t$-blocks above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

Hence in the $n$-free uniform formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable
$O$ and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention,
$61$ agents in the usual $>t$ notation, can always be guaranteed and
$60$ is attained e.g. by $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$,
the star profile $a_{1}=n-3t,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the
familiar $n/4$ first–choice form.  With $j_{0}$ a first-choice
minimiser and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,

$$
c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4,
$$

i.e. the sharp normalised bound $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice voters,
$2(t+1)=42$ in the usual pair formulation, which is the $3t$ uniform
constant written in the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  This is the $n/4$
statement normally quoted in the literature. ∎

1.text:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\,i\in O$.
In particular $b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$ and

$$
\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad|O|(t+1)\le n .
$$

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.
If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $c_{i}=a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only $n$-free obstruction to a set with $|O|\ge2$ is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}\; .
$$

In that regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-saturated uniformly in
$n$ and the only $t$-saturated set which can be forced for every
extension of the first choice numbers is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$,
$c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$.  For this set

$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  Indeed let

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,
$$

and let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three $t$-blocks
$2,3,4$ above the big block $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$

i.e. the whole $n-a_{1}$ block can be made to prefer the same outside
item to $1$.  Hence for a guarantee that has to hold for every $n$ and
every strict profile

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible, the singleton $O_{1}$ being the worst
case.  With $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced to the outside of a suitable $O$ and $3t$
is best possible.  In the $c_{i}>t\iff c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is
the usual $3(t+1)-3$ statement.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free
uniform constant

$$
u_{\min}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, $61$ on the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}\ge t+1$, attained e.g.
by $a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ and the star profile described
above.  In particular on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=
4(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ form $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$, $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ first-choice voters, i.e.
the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same $(m-1)t$ bound.  Up to the
harmless $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ off-by-one this is the $60$-agent,
$21$-first-choice, $n/4$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

4.text:
For a profile put $a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first}(v)\}$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=
a_{j}$.  $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.

* $a_{4}>t$: $O=[4]$ is $>t$-saturated and $b_{j}(O)\equiv0$;
* $a_{3}>t$: $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ satisfies $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$,
$i=1,2,3$, and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
* $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$: $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$,
$i=1,2$, and
$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only obstruction to a $|O|\ge2$ $>t$-saturated set is
$a_{2}\le t$, i.e. $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
In that regime every $|O|\ge2$ can be made to satisfy
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\le t$ and the only set which can be forced to be
$>t$-saturated for every extension of the second and third choices is
the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.

Now $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$ and
$$
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$
and the bound is attainable.  Indeed with
$a_{1}=n-3t$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and every $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$
first and the three $t$-blocks $2,3,4$ above the big block $1$ we have
$c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is
$O_{1}=\{1\}$ and
$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$
For example $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $t=20$, gives
$c_{1}(O_{1})=81>20$ and $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$, $j=2,3,4$.
Hence in the $n$-free uniform formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced outside a $>t$-saturated set and $3t$ is
best possible.  In particular with the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
convention this is the usual $3(t+1)-3$ statement.

For $t=20$ this is the uniform $n$-free guarantee

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting $c_{i}\ge t+1$,
attained by the star profile $a_{1}=n-3t$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.
On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ first-choice form $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$ pair
form of the same $(m-1)t$ bound. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Let $a_{i}$ be the number of first choices of $i$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
For $O\ne\varnothing$ put $c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$,
$j\notin O$. Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can hold only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
In particular $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $b_{j}\equiv0$.
If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ with $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ with $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$, $j=3,4$.
Hence the only truly $n$-free obstruction is $a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.

In that regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be forced to satisfy $\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$
uniformly in $n$, for the adversary can keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ on every
$i\in O\setminus\{1\}$. The only set which can be made $>t$-saturated for
every extension of the second and third choices is the singleton
$O_{1}=\{1\}$, $c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t$.

For $O_{1}$

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,

and the estimate is attainable.  Put

$a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$,

let each $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and let the three $t$-blocks rank
$2,3,4$ above the big block $1$. Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$,
the unique $>t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t$,

e.g. $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$ for
$j=2,3,4$.  The $2t$ and $2(t+1)=42$ pair averages and the $t+1=21$
$n/4$ triple bound are sharp only on the canonical normalisations
$n=2(t+1)$ and $n=4(t+1)=84$. Once $u$ has to work for every $n$ the
singleton regime dominates.

Hence any uniform guarantee must satisfy $u\ge(m-1)t$ and $u=(m-1)t$ is
sufficient.  For $m=4$

$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $3\times20=60$ agents, $3(t+1)-3$ in the strict $>t$ counting,
can always be forced to prefer an outside item to a suitable $O$ and $60$
is best possible in the $n$-free formulation.  On the normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ this is the familiar $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice,
$2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same $(m-1)t$ statement. ∎

$|O|(t+1)\le n$ and $b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.

$b_{j}(O)\equiv0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$.
If $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$,
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$ and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only $n$–free obstruction is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

for then $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–saturated only for $n>4t$ and in
the worst case the only set which can be forced to satisfy
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ for every extension of the second and third
choices is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For $O_{1}$

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the estimate is sharp.  Indeed with

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$–block ranking $i$ first and the three $t$–blocks
above the big block we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every $|O|\ge2$, the
unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

For instance $n=4t+1$, $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ gives
$c_{1}(O_{1})=t+1>t$ and $b_{j}(O_{1})=3t$ for $j=2,3,4$.  Hence

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible for an $n$–free guarantee.  With
$a_{2}>t$ a pair or a triple can be chosen with $\max_{j\notin O}
b_{j}(O)\le2t\le3t$, so the singleton $O_{1}$ is the worst case.

For $m=4$ this is the uniform $n$–free bound

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=3\times20=60$ agents can always be forced to lie
outside a suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible.  In the usual
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict notation this is the familiar $3(t+1)-3$
statement, $61$ agents in the $>t$ counting, attained e.g. by the
star profile $a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$,
for which the only $>t$–saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and
$\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=60$.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar
$n/4$ first-choice form $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$, i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$
pair form of the same $3t$ bound.  This is the $60$, essentially
$21$ first-choice, $(m-1)t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

$$

$$

and for $\emptyset\ne O\subset[m]$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and in the worst
case $c_{i}(O)$ can be made $a_{i}$.  In particular
$b_{j}([m]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$ and

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.

if $a_{3}>t$ we can take $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, with $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
if $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ we can take $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

second and third choices.  The only set which can be guaranteed for
every extension is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For it

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}\le n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1 .
$$

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$-block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three

$|O|\ge2$ and the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ with

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced to the outside of a $>t$-saturated set and
$3t$ is best possible.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3t=60
$$

agents, $61$ in the strict $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, can always be
realised and is attained e.g. by $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$,

$(m-1)t$ expression.  This is the $u=3(t+1)-3=61$ strict $>t$ form

1.text:

b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}([4]\!\setminus\!\{j\})=a_{j}$.  In particular

$$
\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t\Longrightarrow |O|(t+1)\le n,
\qquad c_{i}(O)>t\;{\rm can\;be\;forced\;only\;by\;}a_{i}>t .
$$

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.  Then

* $a_{4}>t$ : $O=[4]$ gives $c_{i}=a_{i}>t$ and $b_{j}\equiv0$;
* $a_{3}>t$ : $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ gives $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$,
  $i=1,2,3$, and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
* $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ : $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ gives $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$,
  $i=1,2$, and
  $$
  b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
  $$

Hence, uniformly in $n$, the only obstruction to a $|O|\ge2$ set with
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

and in that regime the adversary can keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ on
$i\in O\setminus\{1\}$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  The only set which can be
forced to be $>t$-saturated for every extension of the second and third
choices is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$,

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4},
\qquad j\ne1 .
$$

Now $a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$, and the bound is attainable.  Put

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and rank the three $t$-blocks
$2,3,4$ above the big block $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,
$$

e.g. $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $t=20$, gives
$b_{j}(O_{1})=60$, $j=2,3,4$.  Hence

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible in the $n$-free formulation.  With
$a_{2}>t$ the pair or triple above gives $\max b_{j}\le2t\le3t$,
so the singleton $O_{1}$ is the worst case.

For $m=4$ the uniform $n$-free constant is therefore

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=3\times20=60$ agents can always be forced to lie
outside a suitable $O$ and $3t$ is best possible.  In the usual
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict notation this is the $3(t+1)-3$ statement,
$61$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting.

Remark.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
sharp first-choice form is $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$, $c_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$, i.e. the familiar
$n/4$ first-choice, $2(t+1)=42$ pair, form of the same $(m-1)t$ bound.
This is the $21$ first-choice, $42$ pair, $60$-agent statement quoted
in the literature. ∎

For a profile write $a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first}(v)\}$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $\emptyset\ne O$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and in the
worst extension $c_{i}(O)$ can be made $a_{i}$.  In particular
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$ and

$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can be forced only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$
and can be forced in the worst case only for $a_{i}\ge t+1$, $i\in O$.

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}\ge t+1\}$.  

* $a_{4}\ge t+1$: $O=[4]$, $c_{i}\ge t+1$, $b_{j}\equiv0$;
* $a_{3}\ge t+1>a_{4}$: $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$, $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}\ge
t+1$ and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
* $a_{2}\ge t+1>a_{3}$: $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$, $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}\ge t+1$
and

$$
b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
$$

Hence the only $n$–free obstruction to a set with $|O|\ge2$ is

$$
a_{1}\ge t+1\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}\; .
$$

In that regime the adversary can keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ for every
$i\in O\setminus\{1\}$ and the only set which can be forced to satisfy
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ for every extension of the second and
third choices is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n\ge t+1,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the estimate is sharp.  With

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
$$

and every $a_{i}$–block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three
$t$–blocks $2,3,4$ above the big block $1$ we have $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for
every $|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t ,
$$

e.g. $n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ gives
$\max_{j}b_{j}(O_{1})=60$.  Hence in the $n$–free formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t ,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible, the singleton $O_{1}$ being the worst
case.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t
$$

agents can always be forced to lie outside a $>t$–saturated set and
$3t$ is best possible.  In the $c_{i}\ge t+1$ convention this is the
usual $3(t+1)-3$ statement.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{\min}=3\times20=60
$$

agents, $61$ on the strict $>t$ counting, can always be guaranteed and
is attained by the star profile $a_{1}=n-3t$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.
On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ this is the
familiar $n/4$ form $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ first–choice voters,
i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same $(m-1)t$ bound, the $60$
above being its $n$–free expression.  This is the $3t$–$n/4$ bound
quoted in the literature. ∎

agents can always be forced to lie outside a suitable $O$ and $60$ is
best possible, e.g. $a_{1}=n-60,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ with the star
profile $b_{j}(O_{1})=60$, $j=2,3,4$.  This is $61$ agents in the usual
$c_{i}\ge t+1$, $b_{j}\le u$ off-by-one convention, the $n/4=t+1=21$
first-choice, $2(t+1)=42$ pair form on the canonical normalisation

public_text.5:
Write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$,
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}, \qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$b_{j}([4]\setminus\{j\})=a_{j}$.  In particular
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ can be forced only for $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.

* $a_{4}>t$ : $O=[4]$ can be taken, $c_{i}=a_{i}>t$, $b_{j}\equiv0$;
* $a_{3}>t$ : $O_{123}=\{1,2,3\}$ can be taken,
  $c_{i}(O_{123})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2,3$, and $b_{4}(O_{123})=a_{4}\le t$;
* $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$ : $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ can be taken,
  $c_{i}(O_{12})\ge a_{i}>t$, $i=1,2$, and
  $$
  b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,\qquad j=3,4 .
  $$

Hence the only $n$–free obstruction to a set with $|O|\ge2$ which is
$>t$–saturated for every extension of the second and third choices is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}\; .
$$

In that regime no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–saturated uniformly in $n$
and the only set which can be forced to be $>t$–saturated for every
extension is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  Now

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t ,\qquad 
b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le 3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and the estimate is sharp.  With

$$
a_{1}=n-3t,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n>4t,
$$

let every $a_{i}$-block rank $i$ first and let the three $t$-blocks
$2,3,4$ rank above the big block $1$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\le t$ for every
$|O|\ge2$, the unique admissible $>t$-saturated set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t .
$$

For example $n=4t+1$, $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, gives
$c_{1}(O_{1})=t+1>t$ and $b_{j}(O_{1})=3t$, $j=2,3,4$.  With $t=20$
the extremal star is $a_{1}=n-60$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, e.g.
$n=81$, $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, for which the only
suitable set is $O_{1}=\{1\}$ and $\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(O_{1})=60$.

Hence in the $n$-free uniform formulation

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible, the singleton $O_{1}$ being the worst
case.  For $m=4$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t ,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=3\times20=60$ agents can always be forced outside a
suitable $O$ and $60$ is best possible.  In the usual $c_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ strict notation this is the familiar $3(t+1)-3$ statement,
$61$ agents in the $>t$ off-by-one counting.  On the canonical
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=84$ this is the familiar $n/4$ form
$b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ first-choice voters,
i.e. the $2(t+1)=42$ pair form of the same $(m-1)t$ bound. ∎

$$

$$

  $$
  b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t,\qquad j=3,4 .
  $$

Hence, uniformly in $n$, the only obstruction to a $|O|\ge2$ set with
$\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ is

$$
a_{1}>t\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4},
$$

and in that regime the adversary can keep $c_{i}(O)=a_{i}\le t$ on
$i\in O\setminus\{1\}$ for every $|O|\ge2$.  The only set which can be
forced to be $>t$-saturated for every extension of the second and third

$$
c_{1}(O_{1})=n>t,\qquad

\qquad j\ne1 .

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t
$$

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=3\times20=60$ agents can always be forced to lie
outside a suitable $O$ and $3t$ is best possible.  In the usual
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ strict notation this is the $3(t+1)-3$ statement,

Put $k=\max\{r:a_{r}>t\}$.

* $a_{2}>t\ge a_{3}$: $O_{12}=\{1,2\}$ works, $b_{j}(O_{12})\le a_{3}+a_{4}\le2t$.

$b_{j}(O_{1})=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-a_{1}=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}\le3t$.

and the bound is sharp.  The extremal star is $a_1=n-3t$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, every $a_i$-block ranking $i$ first and ranking the three $t$-blocks $2,3,4$ above the big block $1$. Hence for an $n$-free guarantee

$\min_O\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le(m-1)t$,

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible, the singleton $O_1$ being the worst case. For $m=4$
